pending.title: Garage Italia Gives the Fiat 500 an Electric Makeover
pending.summary: The custom shop reimagines the Italian icon as an open-air electric runabout with woven seating, marine-grade materials, and nearly endless ways to make it your own

content.source_text: For yacht owners arriving in a Mediterranean port, finding a way to explore the surrounding town presents a different sort of transportation challenge. Zipping around on a Vespa might sound charming, but not everyone is made for the scooter life. Italian auto custom shop Garage Italia has created its own take on the classic Fiat 500 Spiaggina to give the yachting crowd a stylish alternative for getting around town. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia At its core, the Spiaggina is a humble Fiat 500. The “Cinquecento,” as it’s called in Italian, was created to be to Italy what the Mini Cooper was to Britain and the VW Beetle to Germany: small, basic transportation to bring mobility to the masses in the post-WWII era. The original Fiat 500 Jolly, also known as the Spiaggina, transformed that practical foundation into a doorless, open-air vehicle designed for leisurely drives along the Mediterranean coast. With its distinctive woven seating and removable canopy, it became a fixture of Italian resort culture. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia The Garage Italia remake distinguishes itself from its forebears by using electric power, with a rear-mounted motor delivering 13 horsepower and 60 lb-ft of torque. Hardly muscle-car statistics, but it’s enough to get the convertible up to more than 45 miles per hour. The 11 kWh battery gives it 87 miles of range on the WLTP test cycle. That should be more than enough for short trips around coastal towns, while electric power eliminates the need to carry additional gasoline aboard a yacht. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia But the other way this Jolly stands out is a bit more obvious: it’s extensively customizable. The sheet metal comes in 18 shades (off-menu colors are also an option), and the weather-resistant roof, cushions, and other components are available in dozens of fabric patterns from Italian textile company Mariaflora . The seats are handcrafted by Bonacina , an Italian furniture maker specializing in woven designs since 1889, and are available in natural or tinted rattan or Polycore, a composite material designed to withstand sun and salt exposure. Even the flooring takes its cues from the marine world, using durable, waterproof EVA material from ItalDek . And as with Porsches, Ferraris, and all sorts of other exotic machinery these days, you can configure your ideal version on its maker’s website . Photography courtesy of Garage Italia At €85,000 (around $97,000) before options and taxes, this electric runabout costs roughly as much as a BMW 7-Series. It’s a considerable departure from the Fiat 500’s affordable origins, but practicality has never been the point of the Spiaggina. With its open-air design, handcrafted materials, and seemingly endless customization options, Garage Italia has transformed a humble Italian icon into something closer to a bespoke design object on wheels. Photography courtesy of Garage Italia
content.original_title: Garage Italia Gives the Fiat 500 an Electric Makeover

pending.title: Protected Quick Tunnels: simple accountless authentication for your next dev project
pending.summary: Quick Tunnels now support email authentication. Add --allowed-mail to one cloudflared command, and only the addresses or domains you list can reach your local app. No Cloudflare account required on either side.

content.source_text: We launched Quick Tunnels in 2021 to give developers an easy way to share their latest service, application, or project running in their local development environment. A lot has changed since then, but the core use case remains the same. Your coding agent has just finished the feature. The dev server is up on localhost:5173 , and before you ask, the agent offers to let you try it on your phone. It runs one command and hands you a link: That command starts a Quick Tunnel . cloudflared , Cloudflare's lightweight connector, publishes your local service at a random trycloudflare.com URL. No account, no domain, no cost. Agents now use Quick Tunnels for the same reason people do: they are the shortest path from a local port to a URL. The catch has always been the same. Anyone with the link can open it. Starting with cloudflared 2026.9.3, you can add --allowed-mail to the command, and your Quick Tunnel only lets in the email addresses and domains you choose. Visitors prove they own one of those addresses with a one-time PIN from Cloudflare Access . Nobody, on either side, needs a Cloudflare account. Agents made Quick Tunnels more popular than ever Agents that write code need somewhere to show you the result. Agents that live on a Mac mini at home need to be reachable from your phone. Model Context Protocol servers on a laptop need a public endpoint before a hosted assistant can call them. Each of these needs a URL, and a Quick Tunnel produces one from a single command an agent can run by itself. There is no signup form for it to get stuck on. Add -- output json and every log line becomes a JSON object, so the agent can pick out the URL without scraping text. Since agents took off, Cloudflare Tunnel and Quick Tunnels adoption has grown exponentially. On September 18, 2026, a link to the Quick Tunnels page climbed to the top of Hacker News and gathered more than 800 points and 300 comments. The thread reads like a catalog of agent workflows. One person's AI had found Quick Tunnels on its own to publish a site it had just built. Another called them "insanely helpful when doing agentic work on the go." And one commenter asked this post answers: "how long until someone's agent sets up a tunnel for the world to see one's most sensitive, private and embarrassing information or insecure work-in-progress app?" Control who can access your service Pass an email address to --allowed-mail : Alice opens the URL, enters her email address, types in the code sent to her inbox, and reaches your app. Anyone else is stopped before a single request reaches your machine. You still don't create a DNS record, write a configuration file, or open a dashboard. To let in more people, repeat the flag or allow an entire domain: If you leave out --allowed-mail , nothing changes. Public Quick Tunnels behave exactly as they always have. To change who can get in, stop cloudflared and start a new tunnel. Access ends for everyone the moment the process exits. For a stable hostname or richer rules, such as identity provider groups, use Cloudflare Tunnel with Cloudflare Access. To reach an agent at home from your own devices without any public URL and establish bidirectional connectivity, use Cloudflare Mesh . Make it your agent's default Because protection is a single flag, agents can use it as easily as people can. Add one line to the instructions file your coding agent reads, such as AGENTS.md : From then on, the previews your agent shares should open only for you. Agents don't always follow instructions, so check what it ran: cloudflared prints whether a tunnel uses email authentication and how many rules it holds, without printing the addresses. Start a protected tunnel from Wrangler If you build on Workers, you can start the same kind of tunnel from the latest version of wrangler : Wrangler supports repeated flags, comma-separated values, and wildcard domains, and it removes --allowed-mail values from its debug logs. Cloudflare verifies the email. Your machine decides who gets in. When someone opens a protected URL, they land on the Cloudflare Access sign-in page. They enter their email address, then the one-time PIN sent to that mailbox. Email sign-in is built for people using a browser. That step answers one question only: does this person control this email address? It doesn't decide whether they're welcome. cloudflared makes that decision on your machine by comparing the verified address with the rules you typed. Where does a policy live when there is no account? Separating those two questions is the core of the design. Authentication proves who a visitor is. Authorization decides whether that visitor gets in. Every Cloudflare product that enforces access rules keeps the authorization half in the same place: your Cloudflare account. A Quick Tunnel doesn't have one. So the hard part was never sending someone a code. It was deciding where the guest list should live. We started with four requirements. The design had to: Keep Quick Tunnels accountless, because a signup step would defeat the point of a one-command tunnel. Leave the request path for public Quick Tunnels untouched. Avoid a central policy lookup on every request after a visitor signs in. Protect the privacy of the email addresses developers type into their terminals. Our first idea was to put a Cloudflare Access application in front of every Quick Tunnel hostname. Access already checks visitors before traffic reaches cloudflared , so reusing it looked like the shortest path. But hundreds of thousands of Quick Tunnels can be running at once, many for only a few minutes, and each would need its own application and policy. With no account to own them, we would have had to invent a new namespace and route applications dynamically, just to store a list that lives for an afternoon. Our second idea was to build the whole flow. cloudflared would hold the rules, and a Tunnel service would send and check the codes. The authorization half of this idea was good: each connector checks its own list, which scales naturally and keeps the rules on the developer's machine. The authentication half was not. Sending a code is the easy part of email login. The hard parts are getting email delivered, stopping abuse, building secure challenges, managing sessions, and serving a sign-in page that is accessible and translated, then operating all of it safely for years. Cloudflare Access has already solved those problems. So we kept the best half of each idea. Access verifies that the visitor controls the email address. A small authentication broker running on Cloudflare Workers turns that verified identity into a short-lived, signed handoff. The broker is stateless by design. It stores no tunnel policies, no visitor sessions, and no identity records, and it never sees a tunnel's guest list. cloudflared checks the handoff and makes the authorization decision itself, in memory, against the rules you typed. The result is the property we cared about most: your guest list never leaves your machine. Cloudflare learns that a tunnel requires email authentication. It doesn't learn who you invited. Following a request through a protected Quick Tunnel A protected tunnel is created the same accountless way as a public one. The only extra thing cloudflared sends is the authentication mode, never your rules. If the service doesn't confirm that mode, cloudflared refuses to start rather than hand you a public URL by mistake. The first time a visitor opens the URL: cloudflared sees a request with no session. It redirects the browser to login.trycloudflare.com with a random, single-use state tied to that browser and valid for 10 minutes. Cloudflare Access sends a one-time PIN to the visitor's email address and verifies it. The broker checks the Access identity and returns a short-lived, signed assertion bound to the tunnel hostname and to that state. The browser delivers it in a form POST, so it never lands in a URL, browser history, or logs. cloudflared verifies the assertion, uses up the state, and checks the email against your rules. On a match, it creates a local session and sends the visitor to the page they asked for. Otherwise, the visitor gets a generic response that reveals nothing about the list. Later requests use that session for up to four hours (less if the visitor's Access sign-in expires sooner), or until you stop cloudflared . There is no central lookup and no policy service. The session cookie holds a random value and an expiry time, and nothing about who the visitor is. cloudflared strips authentication credentials before forwarding requests, so your app never sees them and never has to implement a login flow. If any check fails, the request never reaches your local service. A protected tunnel never falls back to public mode. Built by interns Protected Quick Tunnels were shipped by two interns: Hugo Vicente on product and Alessandro Frigerio on engineering. They took it from the product requirements to the authentication broker to the cloudflared release. That's how internships work at Cloudflare: interns own real problems and deliver solutions to production. Try it on your next demo Email protection for Quick Tunnels is free, like Quick Tunnels themselves. Install or update cloudflared , start your local server, and add the --allowed-mail flag: Setup details, matching rules, and limits are in the Quick Tunnels documentation . The next time you or your agent shares what you're building, the link will only open for the people you chose.
content.original_title: Protected Quick Tunnels: simple accountless authentication for your next dev project

content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: carefully tailored leather upholstery takes centre stage in the Nyla executive chair , produced by furniture brand Omidi . Bringing the feeling of a private office wherever it sits, the Nyla leather chair combines a high back, leather upholstery and advanced adjustment controls smoothly integrated into its aluminium alloy base. The Nyla executive chair is upholstered in leather Omidi created the Nyla leather chair out of the belief that true luxury lies not in excess but in refinement, striving to reduce the chair to a clean and balanced silhouette while centring the capability of leather to develop unique character and make an item feel more personal over time. "Omidi's leather executive chair collection focuses on combining refined craftsmanship with modern comfort, offering designs suitable for both professional offices and luxury home workspaces," said the company. The brand's chair's are designed for ergonomic comfort as well as quiet luxury A Gold winner in the MUSE Design Awards, the chair includes integrated armrests to support a natural body position and a sculpted seat made from high-density foam that provides firmness and resilience. The adjustment mechanisms include a gas lift system certified for up to 136 kilograms, 135-degree multi-angle tilt and a sliding seat, while lumbar support supports the natural curve of the spine and reduced pressure on the back over prolonged periods of sitting. pending.title: Introducing Clef-omni with full multimodality, plus a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash
pending.summary: We are expanding the Clef decision model family with Clef-omni, natively processing audio, video, images, and text in a single pipeline. We’ve also lowered Clef-flash pricing and boosted Clef inference speeds by up to 2.0x.

content.source_text: Following last week’s release of Clef and Clef-flash , Cloudflare’s open-weight decision models, we decided to bring forth more gifts. Today, we’re releasing Clef-omni, which takes in audio and video input alongside text and image. We also cut the price of Clef-flash so it is now cheaper than Jev, and we made Clef faster. Although the model game is still early for Cloudflare, innovation and iteration is in our DNA, and we apply these principles to everything we do. In fact, the story of Clef came together over the course of less than a week. We decided we wanted to do something in the decision model space on a Friday evening, trained the model over the weekend, and launched it on Thursday. Even with such a short timeline, we were able to ship performant, high-quality, open-weight models for the community — imagine what more we can do in the future. For today, we’re excited to keep up the momentum with new additions and improvements to our Clef family of models. This is just the beginning, and we’ll continue to get better, faster, cheaper, and more innovative. Clef-omni takes audio, video, image, and text input Our new Clef-omni model is able to take audio, video, image, and text input. This changes the paradigm for decision models, which have been largely text-only since the debut of Jev from TypeSafe. With Clef, we supported images and video frame arrays, but Clef-omni is able to take in audio (wav or mp3) and video (mp4 or webm) alongside text and images. Instead of setting up cascading pipelines of models that transcribe speech-to-text, or splitting audio and image channels from video, you can just call one model to make decisions across any modality. We are now one step closer to a model that is able to interact with the world as we experience it — through audio, visual, and textual communication, all in one. Check out our developer docs for the new Clef-omni model. We also released the model open-weights on HuggingFace . For a quick start, here’s how you can send new modality inputs to Clef-omni: Clef-omni expands our open-weight decision architecture to natively handle multimodal workflows. We built this on a Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct mixture-of-experts (MoE) foundation, where the model was already capable of processing text, imagery, audio, and video directly within a single pipeline. However, we adopt the primary comprehension backbone while discarding the text-to-speech output components. In production, Clef-omni executes a quick prefill pass across the complete payload, scoring all modalities and valid parameter options simultaneously. Because we skip output token generation since Clef models are not Large Language Models (LLMs), we remove the overhead of transcribing or captioning incoming files. Media elements map straight into the unified sequence, where video and audio are synced with visual frames for joint processing. Clef-omni then pulls candidate values directly from internal embeddings using our two-stage attention routing: every valid option gathers key evidence from the input (regardless if they are buried in text snippets, visual elements, or audio streams) before field vectors cross-attend across the full context to compute confidence scores. We add a built-in lexical grammar that preserves option semantics, so that we can deliver fast, schema-constrained scoring across every input type. We train the model with the same techniques as we did with Clef — freezing the Qwen3 backbone, training low-rank adapters (LoRA), and applying our standard post-training approach: combining label-smoothed cross-entropy loss with Brier score calibration. The result is a model that is resilient and designed to succeed regardless of schema variations, field ordering, and prompt structures. This brings several core upgrades to the Clef model family. Calibrated, schema-bound decisions now seamlessly handle text, images, audio, and synchronized video in a single API call. It's also fast. Text-only decisions return in about 130 ms at the median, image inputs in about 150 ms, and audio clips in a few hundred milliseconds. Even a full 21-second video clip with sound is scored in about 1.5 seconds, all in a single API call. Our benchmarking shows strong performance across benchmarks, even with new modalities and MoE architecture. Benchmark Clef-omni Clef Clef-flash Jev BFCL · case exact 98.2 98.47 98.76 95.75 ToolRet · nDCG@10 66.6 69.19 66.43 65.28 API-Bank · accuracy 92.7 91.93 93.11 88.19 Home appliances · case exact 69.3 82.95 97.73 52.27 When2Call · accuracy 63.3 72.37 65.58 80.97 BANKING77 · macro-F1 94.8 94.20 90.93 79.74 CLINC150+OOS · macro-F1 97.7 97.43 66.77 89.27 BRIGHT · nDCG@10 42.0 45.91 39.26 47.52 Amazon ESCI · macro-F1 57.8 57.48 57.39 55.21 PhishNChips · accuracy 73.2 79.60 75.05 62.55 We also benchmarked against the TypeSafe evals to show how Clef-omni performs . Workflow Metric Clef-Omni Clef Clef-flash Jev Invoice processing Exact actions 60.2 64.7 57.1 61.8 Invoice processing Primary action 82.0 86.2 73.3 83.1 Customer service Exact actions 71.6 76.3 77.0 76.0 Security incidents Exact actions 61.7 62.9 61.7 61.7 Agent trace observability Primary action 65.8 68.5 69.8 71.6 Clef-flash model is now cheaper We heard your feedback — you want a decision model affordable enough to incorporate into any workflow. We’ve made a few optimizations and can now offer Clef-flash at cheaper prices. We want Clef to be able to make decisions that scale for you across all your agentic workflows, and now our pricing also incentivizes that. We were able to optimize the model to the point where Clef-flash is now cheaper than Jev while still being performant and high-quality. Check out the developer docs for the most up-to-date pricing information at all times, including more detail on how image and audio modalities are converted to input tokens for pricing. Clef-flash – originally $0.09 per M input tokens, now $0.038 per M input tokens Clef – remains at $0.24 per M input tokens Clef-omni – launched today at $0.15 per M input tokens However, one trade-off we have to make in order to have cheaper pricing is to cut the context window of Clef-flash. The hosted version of Clef-flash now has a context window of 24k, instead of 64k as previously advertised. The model weights on Hugging Face are untouched and were trained to support a 256k context window should you choose to self-host it. From our usage data, we see that only 0.24% of requests exceed 24k input tokens. Based on this data, we decided to make the call to drop the context window to 24k for Clef-flash in order to price it at a more accessible entry point. Our Clef model remains at a 64k context window, and we encourage folks with larger context needs to switch to Clef instead of Clef-flash. Clef model is now faster Speeds are also faster for the Clef model, with new optimizations to the hosted version of Clef on Workers AI. No new model weights are released because most of the optimizations we made are at the serving infrastructure layer, not materially to the model weights or architecture. Check out our new speeds below: Input size Before: median / p95 (ms) Now: median / p95 (ms) Median speedup ~800 tokens 262 / 438 152 / 351 1.7× ~3,400 tokens 616 / 777 305 / 531 2.0× ~16,000 tokens 2,721 / 3,250 1,635 / 1,805 1.7× One of the optimizations we made was to move to SGLang for serving the model. We worked with the SGLang team and made pull requests to incorporate Clef (PR #42721 ), which will be released in SGLang 0.5.22. You can also self-host Clef since we released the weights, and the new SGLang launch commands are available on our updated Hugging Face repo as well as the SGLang cookbooks . How are people using Clef? At Cloudflare, we’ve had teams experimenting with Clef as a model that can help classify over general domains. The coolest thing about watching teams adopt Clef is that the capability to do detections and classifications have moved into the model layer, where it is accessible for anyone to start incorporating decision models into their use cases. Previously, even with zero-shot classifiers, the small models may not have been powerful enough to classify across any domain without further tuning. You might have needed to stand up a specialized machine learning team to help train over your particular domain, and gather a corpus of data in order to train a better model. Now, all you need to do is call a model to instantly parse through input data with precision. A few highlights of how teams at Cloudflare are using Clef: Our public GitHub docs repo uses Clef to instantly detect and close spam issues . EmDash, our content management system, moderates plugin libraries for phishing . Our data loss prevention team is scanning data for potential personally identifiable information (PII) like government IDs. And our threat intelligence team is using Clef to help detect malicious domains. Give it a try! We’re excited to bring you more from the Clef family of models, including new modalities like audio and video, as well as making the model more accessible with cheaper pricing and faster speeds. Clef is fully Jev-API compatible and available via AI Gateway, so it is as simple as changing the model ID to try out Clef today. Check out our developer docs for more information. Thank you for all the love and warm reception around Cloudflare’s first models — we are focused on bringing you more. Try out our Clef family of models, and tell us what you think.

content.source_text: Dezeen Showroom: surfaces brand VitrA Tiles has developed V-Flex, a method of installation that aims to meet evolving architectural expectations by being simple and adhesive-free. The company's V-Flex system provides a quick and simple installation option for projects that seek efficiency, the flexibility to make changes over time, or the ability to preserve the existing floor beneath. V-Flex allows for quick, adhesive-free installation The system uses Välinge’s Ceraloc locking technology, with tongue-and-groove edges that allow tiles to slot into place, enabling precise alignment and even grout lines with reduced drying time. In addition, the installation method provides good acoustic performance. The V-Flex method provides flexibility VitrA Tiles recommends this method for use when installing tiles in interiors spanning retail spaces, showrooms, offices, hotels, education facilities and commercial spaces. content.source_text: Meta has revealed slimline VR glasses for immersive entertainment on the go and an audio-only, camera-free version of its Ray-Ban glasses as the latest additions to its expanding product portfolio. Announced by CEO Mark Zuckerberg last night at the technology company's annual Connect conference, the Meta VR Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses expand its market-leading range of eyewear and headsets. The Meta VR Glasses represent the bigger breakthrough, bringing virtual-reality gaming, 3D movies and other immersive digital experiences into a form factor only slightly larger than an ordinary pair of glasses. Meta's VR Glasses are slimmed down from previous headset form factors This allows them to be worn for longer than current headsets and carried on the daily commute, as people might do with a pair of over-ear headphones. Meta says it achieved the lightweight construction by splitting the architecture into two: the glasses, weighing about 100 grams, plus an attached "puck" that clips onto a pocket or bag and handles the processing. Also key are the glasses' ultra-compact pancake lenses, which are about the size of a Scrabble tile and are fixed within a soft mesh structure on the inside of the frames. They have a two-part architecture with an attached puck The wearer manually shifts these lenses to sit directly in front of their eye, filling everything but their peripheral view with a 5K display. This micro-OLED display offers angular resolution of 37 pixels per degree – more than Meta's current market-leading Quest VR headsets and enough to deliver crisp text and rich imagery. The Meta VR Glasses can be used to play games or watch entertainment from the Meta Quest platform, including movies recorded in or converted to 3D. There are also new immersive formats that Meta is pioneering, like "immersive sports" streamed in ultra-high definition from the edge of the playing field at live events. Ultra-compact lenses deliver high-resolution viewing Users navigate the operating system using their eyes, voice and natural hand gestures like swiping and pinching, without having to use controllers – in some cases even to play entire games. Meta also envisions the VR Glasses being used for work. Using full-colour passthrough – the view of the world in front of the glasses that's captured through its outward-facing cameras – wearers can turn any table surface into a keyboard and touchpad and surround themselves with multiple virtual screens from their Mac or PC. The VR Glasses will deliver up to three hours of continuous media playback from the battery on the puck. Meta expects to put the device on sale in spring 2027. The VR Glasses are for work as well as play Unlike the rest of Meta's eyewear offering, the VR glasses are not intended to be worn all the time or to be used primarily for AI assistance, although the company's new Muse AI will be built-in. The use of Meta's AI glasses out on the street has earned them the nickname of "pervert glasses" , due to various documented incidents of men using the barely visible camera to covertly film women. Surveillance concerns were also amplified after a Swedish news investigation revealed that videos captured by wearers' cameras – including highly sensitive ones where they were nude or having sex – were being streamed to subcontractors in Kenya . Read: "Big Tech is using design philosophy as a smokescreen" The pushback against these aspects of the technology may be a driver behind Meta's other key new product launch at Connect, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses. Developed with long-term partners EssilorLuxottica, these glasses lack the controversial camera of other Meta models, as well as the small screen of the Meta Ray-Ban Displays , launched this time last year. Their functionality is more limited, letting users listen to audio through small open‑ear directional speakers built into the frame and interact by voice with Meta's AI assistant. Audio-only AI glasses are also in the new lineup The slimmer feature set has allowed Meta to introduce new slimmer styles like the partially wire-frame Ray-Ban Clubmaster. The glasses' 12-hour battery life and 43-gram weight also mean they can more easily be worn all day. In addition to the new products, Meta revealed the Gen 3 version of its Ray-Ban Meta glasses, with three new frame silhouettes, and several new versions of the cheaper Meta Glasses , launched just three months ago, including one with pop star Lisa, whose influence is partly responsible for the Labubu craze. The VR Glasses are designed for portability and comfortable wear The keynote presentation also detailed the expanding capabilities of its Muse "personal AI agent", which was first revealed two weeks ago and which the company will be adding to all of its glasses. At the end, there was a quick sneak peek at a new Tamagotchi-like Muse Charm gadget. Meta has established itself as the dominant player in the small but growing market for AI glasses, accounting for 94 per cent of display-less AI glasses shipped in the first half of 2026, according to tracking by Counterpoint Research . By the end of the year, it will have more than 100 different styles available in its Ray-Ban, Oakley and own-brand collections. content.source_text: Designer Lee Broom has created an "atmospheric environment" in his Shoreditch showroom with The Chant Chambers, an installation showcasing his glass-block Chant lighting collection at London Design Festival . The Chant Chambers displays the modular light in a variety of forms – as a portable lamp, wall lamp, linear pendants and oversized chandeliers. Lee Broom added plinths and sculptures to his showroom All are presented inside Broom 's showroom, where textured vertical screens create a series of interconnected spaces designed to have a cinematic atmosphere. The Chant Chambers, which Broom described as "an elegant yet surreal lounge," has wood-panelled walls and tactile wall-to-wall carpeting and features stone plinths and a number of sculptures. Wood panels and textured screens divide the space "I wanted the Chant Chambers to feel like an atmospheric environment rather than a display of individual lights," Broom told Dezeen. "The installation explores how the same cubic form can be transformed as it is repeated across a space, using different configurations to create a sense of discovery," he continued. "It also reflects the way our clients are looking for lighting that can be adapted specifically to their interiors rather than choosing a single fixed object." Glass-cube pendants were hung in lines to create an architectural feel Broom also used Chant lights in linear arrangements as geometric ceiling designs with an architectural feel. The moody, smoky colour palette of the installation was inspired by Chant's latest iteration – a smoked-glass finish in a darker tone than the previous design. Read: Lee Broom displays "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico City art week debut "The new smoked glass finish was a starting point for the concept," Broom said. "It has a depth and warmth that works particularly well with the design of Chant and it nods to the late 1970s, early 80s period when glass blocks were very prevalent in modern architecture." "The palette was developed around those darker, richer tones to create a space that feels alluring and atmospheric, while still allowing the geometry of the lighting to stand out," he continued. Broom drew on 1970s interiors for the installation Glamorous 1970s interiors have been making a comeback, with a number of designers looking to the decade for their interiors, as seen recently in a Marseille wine bar . Broom believes that his Chant light has played a part in this trend, especially when it comes to bringing geometric forms and glass blocks back into contemporary interiors. "Since I first introduced the original Chant Chandelier in 2022, those references have gained real momentum," he said. "What interests me is reinterpreting them rather than simply recreating the 1970s, giving those nostalgic materials a more contemporary expression." Wall sconces also decorate the space He argues that these types of interiors also help put the focus on the lighting. "This kind of aesthetic really allows lighting to take centre stage, not just through the fixtures themselves, but through the ambience they create," Broom said. At the end of The Chant Chambers installation, Broom placed a three-tier Chant chandelier to fully showcase the lighting collection. A three-tiered chandelier completes the installation The designer has previously created a "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico Design Week and a chandelier installation for last year's London Design Festival . The photography is by Luke Hayes. The Chant Chamber is on show at 95 Rivington Street, EC2A 3AY, from 15 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week. content.source_text: 삼성전자가 유럽 빌트인 가전 주요 시장인 독일에 상설 쇼룸을 개관하며 유럽 시장 공략에 속도를 낸다. 삼성전자는 유럽의 대표 주방 가구·가전 B2B 행사인 ‘KM 퀴헨마일레(Küchenmeile)’가 매년 열리는 독일 뢰네 지역에 상설 쇼룸을 마련해 현지 주방 가구 업체 및 파트너들과의 접점을 강화한다. 퀴헨마일레는 약 300개의 브랜드와 2만 5천 명의 업계 관계자가 참여하는 대규모 주방 가구 행사로, 올해는 19일부터 25일까지 열린다. 삼성전자는 2018년부터 이 행사에 참가해 프리미엄 빌트인 가전을 꾸준히 선보여 왔으며 올해는 행사 기간에 맞춰 상설 쇼룸을 개관했다. 삼성전자는 새 쇼룸을 ▲제품 전시 ▲비즈니스 상담 ▲교육 공간으로 활용하며, 현지 파트너사와의 협업을 본격적으로 확대하고 유럽 빌트인 가전 사업 기반을 강화해 나갈 방침이다. 새 쇼룸은 독일 주방 가구 업체들이 밀집한 뢰네 중심부의 ‘키친 센터 뢰네(Kitchen Center Löhne,KCL)’ 1층에 약 480㎡(약 145평) 규모로 조성됐다. 삼성전자는 제품 전시 공간을 AI 기반의 스마트 주방 콘셉트로 구성해, 방문객들이 제품과 스마트싱스(SmartThings) 플랫폼이 유기적으로 연동되는 삼성 빌트인 가전을 직접 경험할 수 있도록 했다. ▲‘스페이스 맥스(Space Max)’ 기술을 적용해 콤팩트한 외관을 유지하면서도 넓은 내부 공간을 제공하는 ‘비스포크 AI 1도어 냉장고’와 빌트인 상냉장∙하냉동 냉장고 ▲‘AI 맞춤 세척’ 기능으로 오염도를 분석해 헹굼 횟수와 세척 온도를 자동으로 조절해주는 ‘비스포크 AI 식기세척기’ ▲인덕션 중앙에 후드를 내장해 조리 시 발생하는 연기와 냄새를 효과적으로 제거하고 공간활용도를 높인 ‘후드일체형 인덕션’ ▲‘AI 프로 쿠킹’ 기능이 탑재돼 내부 카메라가 식재료를 인식하고 맞춤형 레시피를 제안하는 ‘비스포크 AI 오븐’ 등 최신 주방 가전 라인업을 전시했다. 유럽 주방 환경을 고려한 다양한 가전 설치 솔루션도 전시했다. 식기세척기 상부에 쿡탑을 설치해 주방 공간을 효율적으로 활용하는 솔루션과 최대 12kg의 가구 도어 패널을 식기세척기에 부착해 주방 가구와의 일체감을 높이는 솔루션을 전시했다. 또 우드∙화이트∙네이비 등 다양한 색상의 주방 가구 마감재와 조화를 이루는 빌트인 주방 가전 패키지를 함께 전시해, 주방 가구 업체와 파트너들이 다양한 주방 환경에 적합한 제품 조합과 설치 솔루션을 직접 비교하고 선택할 수 있도록 했다. 삼성전자 DA사업부 이상직 부사장은 “독일 쇼룸 개관은 유럽 빌트인 가전 사업 확대를 위한 중요한 이정표”라며 “현지 파트너들이 삼성의 빌트인 제품과 연결 경험을 직접 체험할 수 있는 쇼룸을 통해 협업을 확대하고, 유럽 시장에서 프리미엄 브랜드 입지를 강화해 나갈 것”이라고 말했다. ▲ 삼성전자가 독일 뢰네에서 빌트인 가전 상설 쇼룸을 개관했다. ▲ 독일 뢰네에 개관한 삼성 빌트인 가전 상설쇼룸에서 방문객이 ‘비스포크 AI 패밀리허브’ 냉장고를 체험하고 있다. ▲ 독일 뢰네에 개관한 삼성 빌트인 가전 상설쇼룸 주방공간에서 담당자가 조리 시연을 하고 있다. ▲ 독일 뢰네에 개관한 삼성 빌트인 가전 상설쇼룸에서 방문객들이 제품을 살펴보고 있다. ▲ 독일 뢰네에 개관한 삼성 빌트인 가전 상설쇼룸에서 담당자와 방문객이 제품 기능 상담을 진행하고 있다.

content.source_text: On the heels of London Design Festival , we have rounded up a selection of furniture and products presented during the city-wide event made of scraps that would otherwise have gone to waste. London Design Festival (LDF) concluded on Sunday, after a week of product launches, exhibitions and installations that showed the best of the capital's design scene. Throughout the event, a slew of designers unveiled projects using materials leftover from manufacturing, whether as an attempt to slash costs, preserve resources or simply experiment visually. Here are seven examples of the trend spotted during London's biggest design week: Top: photo by Lewis Duckworth. Above: photo by Carmel King Dagwood Bench by Lewis Duckworth Lewis Duckworth is one of London's many emerging talents. As the co-founder of guerrilla collective Design Everything , he is always looking for ways to create furniture with the inevitable limitations that come with being a young, independent designer. Dagwood Bench is one such project, made from timber end pieces leftover from furniture production, which are often too narrow or short to be reused and would normally go to waste. Duckworth created the bench from a single laminated plank, sandwiched between two timber faces. The designer explained that offcuts were arranged within these pieces of wood to create a form that "appears visually thick while remaining lightweight and structurally capable". "This project explores ways to re-evaluate these 'un-usable' elements by incorporating them into a larger, cohesive material system," he said. "Given that they started as an industrial byproduct, it felt most appropriate to reprocess them in a standardised format". Duckworth's Dagwood Bench is among the 34-strong shortlist of buildings, furniture and objects nominated for a 2026 Wood Award . A selection of these designs was on display at the Material Matters exhibition during LDF. Second Song by Spared Second Song is a selection of bird-shaped collectible objects by Brighton-based design studio Spared . The studio is known for transforming waste generated by its varied clients into furniture and products, such as tables made from old coffee grounds developed for the Corner cafe at London's Tate Modern museum. Cast using a selection of bio-based binders, the collectible birds were made of offcuts ranging from shell and stone to workshop sawdust and thin scrapings from the surfaces of plastic chopping boards used in industrial kitchens. Second Song was another project presented at Material Matters. Photo courtesy of Out of Worky Tissue box by Tom Golland This statement tissue box was part of Out of Worky , an exhibition of bespoke pieces made using scrap materials that the participants had collected over years of taking on myriad jobs as emerging designers. Tom Golland combined offcuts of walnut and white oak to form the unusually tall tissue dispenser, which is held together with two zinc-plated steel bolts. The show was presented by The Worky , a collective founded by Marley Wellings, Jake Robertson, Kieran Slater and Milo Tonry-Brown. Photo courtesy of Design Everything Chair by Oscar Warman Dubbed "everything I could find in my shed", this timber chair by emerging designer Oscar Warman is a Frankenstein-like hodgepodge of old pieces of furniture that were partially damaged. The chair features a duo of rotten and frayed front legs, which had to be cut and altered. This meant that Warman needed to source a strong piece of timber for the back legs, which he found in the form of part of a shelf that he "cannibalised" by taking it off the wall and using it alongside its brackets. "By designing in this way I spent time mocking up and offering each part to one another to try and resemble a chair shape," said Warman. "I like how few processes were used in the making of this piece and the time was spent problem solving how to make them function as a chair." The chair is still on display as part of Design Everything's With Limitations show at Aram Gallery, which runs until 10 October. Photo courtesy of Design Everything Fused by Audra Grays and Maxim Lester Fused is one of a handful of lamps made by emerging designers Audra Grays and Maxim Lester , who, quite literally, fused together different material offcuts from their respective practices to create lighting. After Lester came across Grays's decorative glass experiments on Instagram, the designers combined the glass offcuts with scrap metal and electrical back boxes found in Lester's workshop. LED strips were pulled from old lamps to illuminate the pieces. Also displayed at Aram Gallery, the rectilinear sconce lights are not the only pieces the duo made from offcuts that were on show during LDF. The pair also presented a chunky desk lamp as part of the Kiln Shift exhibition by Clink Street Ceramics. Photo courtesy of Max Radford Gallery Graywacke OffCut Chair by Carsten in der Elst Based in Cologne, designer Carsten in der Elst has spent the last six years utilising "the full potential of industrial by-product material" when crafting pieces of furniture. Central to In der Elst's portfolio is his Graywacke Offcut series – monolithic tables and chairs made from rough-hewn lumps of stone salvaged from a quarry in Lindlar, western Germany. One of these ancient-looking chairs was presented as part of the Progressive Permanence exhibition by Max Radford Gallery at the Christopher Farr showroom in Shoreditch. Photo courtesy of Design Everything Coat rack by Duy Huynh Emerging designer Duy Huynh is another exhibitor showing as part of With Limitations, who is presenting a timber coat rack made from offcuts salvaged from a stand he crafted to show work at his recent degree show. The size of each piece of wood, reassembled by the designer, was determined by where the previous joints had been cut to create the stand. "This piece is a bit smaller than a conventional coat rack, but I wanted to keep that acknowledgement of where it came from to show the idea that if we treat our materials right, they can serve us for a long time," said Huynh. London Design Festival 2026 took place at various locations around the city from 12 to 20 September. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. pending.title: Bridging technical depth and usability: The story behind Radar’s redesign
pending.summary: We redesigned Cloudflare Radar to make real-time global traffic and outage data accessible to a wider audience — including journalists, less technical researchers, and everyday users. By introducing an interactive map and standardized components, we simplified navigation while preserving technical depth.

content.source_text: Radar provides a real-time view into global Internet trends, powered by Cloudflare’s global network. We support Cloudflare’s mission to help build a better Internet by making web data visible, clear, and actionable for everyone. Since launching in 2020 , Radar has found a natural audience amongst expert users with technical backgrounds, such as network operators and academic researchers who rely on Radar data to observe industry trends and global events. But Radar also has the potential to be a more regular, self-serve resource for journalists, human rights advocates and policymakers, and everyday users. Making Radar accessible to a wider audience is a core part of our vision, so we knew it was time to reevaluate the user experience: How could we make Radar more approachable to broader audiences, while preserving the depth and rigor that we currently have? In this blog post, we’ll introduce the redesigned Radar, share our design process, and outline our broader vision for the platform’s future. Challenges with the previous design While the previous landing page was successful at showing the breadth of Radar’s data, the way that information was presented made it difficult to parse. The bento box layout gave everything similar visual weight, the vertical cards disrupted natural reading patterns, and the styling felt disconnected from Cloudflare’s broader brand. We heard this from users. One external user mentioned that one of his biggest frustrations with Radar was that it was difficult to show to his students. That feedback reinforced the problem that Radar could feel intimidating to people encountering it for the first time. With this in mind, we wanted to create a landing page experience that shaped a clearer path through the content, instead of asking users to interpret everything at once. But making Radar more accessible wasn’t only about reorganizing the content. It was also about making the experience feel more connected to Cloudflare. For external users, consistency directly affects trust and usability. A more cohesive Cloudflare experience helps signal that Radar is an authoritative source, while familiar layout patterns reduce the effort required to move through complex information. Introducing Radar’s new landing page The new and improved Radar uses a visual reference that users of all backgrounds will have a familiarity with — a map. Even though in many ways the Internet operates outside the concept of national borders, its relevance to everyday life is often best understood through geography. The top section focuses on traffic and outages. We lead with outages as they are one of the most concrete, timely, and salient data points about the state of the Internet. Traffic, meanwhile, communicates the scale and breadth of Radar’s data. The map also acts as a navigation point into the insights below, guiding users from the global view into specific countries, trends, and data stories. Below the map, we turned the old bento box chart widgets into a tabbed flow that helps users move through the data more deliberately. The tabs provide summary statistics to give the user a sense of Radar’s capabilities, while also giving them a call to action to explore the data in depth. The tabbed structure creates a clearer hierarchy, keeps the page from feeling overwhelming, and previews the range of information Radar provides. From concept to reality Developing Radar’s design language To develop Radar’s design language, we looked across Cloudflare’s content ecosystem, which exist in these three pillars: Marketing pages (like cloudflare.com) Content experiences, like the Cloudflare Blog and Developer Docs Product experiences Where does Radar fit? Ultimately, we decided that Radar sits at the intersection of all three. At its core, Radar is a data product, but it’s also public-facing and inherently content-rich. The strategy blends design aspects of all three: approachable like marketing, structured and navigable like content, and maintainable by migrating to Kumo components used by Cloudflare’s product system. What we tried along the way From the outset, we knew the landing needed to communicate Radar’s global perspective. Because Radar helps people understand Internet activity across countries and regions, a map felt like the clearest way to make that scope immediately visible. The map went through many rounds of iteration as we tried to strike the right balance between data richness and approachability. Early versions were too dense — we were trying to convey credibility through data-heavy visuals. Later versions moved too far toward marketing-style visuals; they felt more approachable, but risked making Radar’s fresh data feel static or overly summarized. The current direction sits between those two poles: it has the feel of live data, but it’s easier to read. The Radar vision and evolution Because Cloudflare sits in front of roughly 20% of all web traffic, Radar has the opportunity to tell unique and compelling stories about the Internet. To unlock that value, we want to empower every user with real-time insights across security, performance, and traffic. This redesign is a foundational step in that direction. Moving forward, Radar will continue to focus on tools, visualizations, and storytelling frameworks that remove friction for new audiences while doubling down on our deep data infrastructure. By pairing our technical rigor with a cleaner, human-centered experience, we are ensuring that more people can explore, understand, and share the state of the Internet. Help us make Radar better This redesign is our first step toward a more intuitive, scannable Radar. But we're just getting started, and we need your input. What’s working? What isn’t? What insights are still hard to uncover? You can share feedback with us on social media at @CloudflareRadar on X, radar.cloudflare.com on Bluesky, or email us at radar@cloudflare.com .
content.original_title: Bridging technical depth and usability: The story behind Radar’s redesign

content.source_text: Canada's Ivy Studio has transformed a 1970s bank into a veterinary clinic for exotic animals in Laval, Quebec, featuring minimalist interiors and soft lighting. The Fauna clinic occupies a standalone structure completed in a brutalist style near the waterfront, just over the Prairies River northwest of Montreal. Consultation rooms at Fauna are offset from one another and fronted by sweeping walls Ivy Studio leaned into the building's existing style to inform the interiors, creating a calm, minimalist environment for the patients and their handlers. "By celebrating its historical shell, Fauna establishes a unique dialogue between imposing institutional architecture and the compassionate, soothing nature of veterinary care," the studio said. The staggered motif is also applied to the walnut reception counter The building spans 380 square metres over two levels, with the public areas and treatment facilities housed across the ground floor. Boasting 16-foot (4.9-metre) ceilings, the reception and waiting areas maximise natural light from the building's existing windows. The building's tall, coffered ceilings allow for dramatic architectural features The original concrete coffered ceiling is left exposed and painted a deep brown, contrasting concrete flooring and the warm grey of the textured plaster walls. Facing the waiting area, the four consultation rooms are arranged in an offset row through the centre of the plan. Fluted glass doors slide open to the consultation rooms Each is faced with a curved wall that sweeps up to the tall ceiling, mimicking the building's exterior, and is also denoted by vertical partitions with stepped end-profile details. "This dramatic gesture provides intimacy for the consultation rooms while serving as a sculptural focal point from the waiting area," said Ivy Studio. Walnut desks with chrome bases match the benches in the waiting ares Fluted glass doors slide open to access the consultation rooms, which feature walnut desks with chrome bases, matching the waiting room benches and the reception counter. The individual rooms all link to the treatment area behind, where a spiral staircase leads down to office, storage and research space in the basement. Read: Ivy Studio converts historic bank building into offices for Montreal ad agency Careful consideration was given to the lighting design, comprising diffused light boxes inside the consultation rooms along with the natural illumination in the other public spaces. "A soothing environment is paramount for an exotic animal clinic, where patients are easily stressed," Ivy Studio said. "The lighting strategy in the public zones is soft, dimmed, and strictly indirect." A spiral staircase leads down to a staff area in the basement In the treatment room and basement, the building's concrete bones are exposed, and the fluted concrete walls are painted soft cream. The bank's original vault is repurposed as a closed pharmacy and lab – the finishing touch in adapting the former financial institution into a contemporary medical facility. The original bank vault is repurposed as a closed pharmacy and lab Ivy Studio is perhaps best known for its hospitality projects across Canada, with completed restaurant projects ranging in style from Japanese minimalism to colourfully retro and bold and glamorous . The studio's commercial portfolio includes a dry cleaners modelled on a Parisian apartment , an all-black spinning studio and offices for a digital advertising agency also housed in a former bank. content.source_text: Sewn paper and hand-hammered steel sit side by side in these lighting pieces and stools by designer Jesse Butterfield, displayed during London Design Festival 2026. The aptly named Sew Paper Lighting and Stool Des Pois series premiered during Butterfield 's A Veil Boundary exhibition, curated by Alex Tieghi-Walker , in the city-wide festival's Brompton Design District . A series of stools and paper lighting comprised the exhibition The paper lanterns continue the centuries-old tradition of using the material to make lampshades, as a result of its physical lightness as well as its translucency. To realise the Sew Paper Lighting series, Butterfield teamed up with The Paper Foundation , a Lake District-based paper mill, founded by sixth-generation papermaker Mark Cropper. Light shades are stitched together "We got to visit The Paper Foundation and see their process, then select six or seven different papers," said Butterfield. "We went through their archive and chose what we thought would have nice drapage and lighting effects, as well as selecting different papers for different applications." The paper used in the lamps is handmade in the Lake District Slim stainless steel frames dictate each piece's general form and purpose: from pendants and wall lights to floor and table lamps. Beyond this, the lanterns strewn around the space comprise folded, draped and otherwise physically manipulated handmade paper, hand-stitched into amorphous shapes. Read: RCA design students exercise restraint in One Tool One Stool exhibition In dialogue with the paper lamps, Butterfield's Stool Des Pois series explores the sheet metal's capacity to behave in a similar way to paper. A paper model was the natural starting point for the stool, which was then scaled up and recreated in steel, heated and hammered by hand until a thinness and lightness akin to paper was achieved. The stools are decorated with a hammered texture and singed spots The stools are based on the same initial model and dimensions, with natural variations owing to their handmade nature, ensuring that no two are entirely alike. Further distinction is made through the polka dot patterning, a result of intentional blackening of the metal which introduces further visual interest while telling the story of their manufacturing process. Both items feature elements made from or informed by paper and metal "This is the first time where I'm leaving the dots on the surface," said Butterfield. "They come from the making process – in the past I've sanded them away, but I wanted to bring them in now as they fit with the theme of things being perfectly imperfect," he added, nodding to the leitmotif of this year's Brompton Design District programme. Elsewhere in the district, RCA students exhibited a series of stools created with a single tool and Isamaya French launched her second-ever Studio Iron show . The photography is by Andy Stagg . A Veil Boundary was on show from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival . See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. The post Jesse Butterfield marries paper and metal in A Veiled Boundary exhibition appeared first on Dezeen .

pending.title: 1. Creating a Role That Didn’t Exist Before
pending.summary: Learn how Toss’s Technical Writers have expanded their role from writing documentation to designing knowledge systems for the organization.

content.source_text: *This is the English version of a previously published article . Hi, I’m Juyeon Han, Technical Writing Chapter Lead at Toss. In this series, I’ll share how Technical Writers (TWs) at Toss have expanded our role from simply writing documentation to designing the systems that manage knowledge across the organization. “Why is this built this way?” It’s the kind of question you hear, and ask, all the time at work. Maybe you track down the person who wrote the code and try to piece together what they remember. Maybe you dig through a year-old thread for context. And sometimes, there’s simply no one left to ask. As we rely more on AI, this problem becomes even harder to ignore. AI may know a lot about the world, but it doesn’t know the context and history unique to your organization. So every time you ask it to do something, you have to fill in the gaps. People often say that code is the Single Source of Truth (SSoT). But code only preserves the outcome . It can tell you what something does, but not necessarily why it was built that way or what decisions led to it. Most of us have probably stared at uncommented code at some point, trying to figure out how we got there. That’s why I believe documentation matters as much as ever. A true SSoT is only complete when you have both the code and the context surrounding it . Ultimately, we’re the ones who have to explain why the code is the way it is. If we want AI to work with what we know, we first have to capture that knowledge somewhere. And that’s the gap the Technical Writing Chapter has been working to fill. But our job isn’t simply to write documents that fill in the missing context. Looking at what TWs do today, the role has changed significantly since I first joined Toss five years ago. Our goals have changed, too. This year, we’re working toward a system where knowledge builds up on its own. And the ultimate goal of the Technical Writing Chapter is to make ourselves unnecessary . When I first thought about how AI might change our work, I assumed Technical Writers would be among the first to be replaced. But I couldn’t have been more wrong. If anything, our work has expanded. So how did we get from writing technical docs to designing knowledge systems, with the ultimate goal of making ourselves unnecessary? From Writing Documents to Bringing Knowledge to People When I first started working on internal documentation at Toss, one of my first projects was creating onboarding documents for our Frontend Chapter. But as I worked on internal docs, something kept bothering me. To me, the goal of Technical Writing isn’t to produce great writing. It’s to help readers solve problems and accomplish what they need to do . And no matter how good a document is, people rarely read it from beginning to end. They look for the one thing they need. I do the same. So I started thinking: instead of writing a document and sending people a link, how could we make sure the knowledge inside it actually gets used? That question led to Mr. Park (박씨) , a chatbot we built. (*Refer to TMC25 ) It lets people ask questions conversationally from the messaging tools and IDEs they already use, then answers based on our existing documentation, with sources included. Instead of asking people to go find the documentation, we brought the documentation to them. What happened next was interesting. People who had never been particularly interested in writing (or reading) documentation started coming to us. “We want something like this for our chapter.” “Could we build this for our organization too?” As Toss grew, people were getting tired of getting the same questions over and over. They wanted a way to retrieve institutional and tacit knowledge from a system. At the same time, rapid advances in AI were making documentation more important than ever. If we wanted AI to understand our work and actually be useful, we first had to give it the knowledge and context to work with. Documentation had long been treated as a chore. Suddenly, everyone wanted it. It was fascinating to watch. And amid that shift, I started building a knowledge system that everyone at Toss could use. I’ll cover that product in more detail in the next article. From Documentation to Knowledge Systems That was when we began to push beyond the traditional boundaries of Technical Writing. We realized our role could no longer stop at documentation. We needed to become people who design knowledge systems tailored to the needs of different organizations. And as AI takes on more and more work, capturing the knowledge and tacit context scattered across the organization has become more important than ever. A well-designed knowledge system makes the entire organization more productive while helping every team member get up to speed quickly. As organizations grow, questions multiply and communication becomes increasingly costly. A strong knowledge system is critical for maintaining both the speed and quality of how we work . Knowledge is verified information that helps an individual or organization understand a problem or situation, make better decisions, and take action. Information only becomes knowledge when it has been validated within that context. A knowledge system is the structure that brings that knowledge together and delivers it to the people, and AI, that need it, when they need it. Knowledge scattered across code, conversations, deployments, and other sources is brought together into a Single Source of Truth. It’s then structured so that it can be understood not only by people but also by AI, and immediately put to use through questions, workflows, and automation. Today, the work of the Technical Writing Chapter at Toss falls into four main areas. First, we build products . We lead the team that builds and operates todoc, our internal knowledge management platform. Second, we embed ourselves in different organizations and lead their documentation efforts . We bring together scattered knowledge in ways tailored to each organization and make that knowledge as useful as possible. There’s no one-size-fits-all knowledge system, so we adapt our approach to each organization. Third, we eliminate the manual Technical Writing work . Through AI workflows and automation, we’re building ways for anyone to create and review documentation at a consistently high level. Finally, we build a culture of documentation across Toss . We run community-wide sessions on topics such as how to write documentation that AI can understand effectively. We also run documentation guilds and knowledge committees within individual organizations, changing how knowledge is captured and managed throughout Toss. What We’ll Cover in This Series Here’s what we’ll explore in the rest of the series: Beyond Our Expertise : How our expertise in Technical Writing found its way into todoc, the knowledge product we built. Why Documentation Never Seems to Stick / Same Problem, Different Solutions (Korean version only): In two interviews, we’ll share how we approached a problem nearly every company faces: knowledge that never seems to accumulate, and what we learned along the way. Technical Writers, Planning Our Own Disappearance (Korean version only): Can Technical Writing be automated? We’ll share what we’ve built so far. Becoming Knowledge Experts (Korean version only): Explore our ultimate goal of enabling organizations to create and manage knowledge on their own, without Technical Writers. Our job title is still “Technical Writer.” But the work we actually do today is much closer to designing an organization’s knowledge infrastructure. We didn’t set out to redefine the role. We simply followed the problems that needed solving, and ended up redrawing the boundaries of the job along the way. Before we knew it, we had created a role that didn’t quite exist anywhere else in the industry. And this shift isn’t unique to Technical Writing. AI is redefining the work of every profession. In such an environment, anyone can expand the boundaries of their role. Our chapter started with one person. Now there are three of us, and we’re looking for more people to join us. Over the course of this series, we’ll share how we got here, one story at a time.
content.original_title: 1. Creating a Role That Didn’t Exist Before

content.source_text: The "dopamine decor" interiors trend is taking social media by storm, but it's just another disingenuous dressing-up of superficial style as life-improving experience, writes Julie Lasky . For some time now, the internet has labeled a maximalist decorating trend that embraces candy colors, fuzzy textures and whimsical furnishings "dopamine decor". The reference is, of course, to neuroscience, and supporters claim that the style, which, like many interiors ideas, has its roots in fashion, produces a genuine emotional uplift. The look is energetic and often charming. Seen on social media, it leaves a stubborn pink glow in the mind as one moves on to a cake-fail video. For every white-paint-loving minimalist, there has always been a Barbie with a hot-pink dream house Books celebrate it, too. In April, Rachel Varney, who has an Instagram called The Shoestring Home , published Dopamine Home (Mobius) . The publicist described it as "the ultimate mood-boosting guide filled with color know how, creative hacks and cost saving tips and tricks". The central image on the bubblegum-pink cover is of a squiggle-based glass coffee table supporting a ceramic fruit bowl shaped like a bunch of bananas. And now, Maitri Mody, a New York-based designer whose Instagram is called Honey I Dressed the Pug , is coming out in late August with Dopamine Design: Creating a Home That Makes You Happy (Ten Speed Press) . Her goal is to teach readers that they are not chained to conformity but can break away and pursue their own idiosyncratic, ecstatic visions. "For years, design trends worshiped minimalism ," Mody writes, in prose that has the rhythmic cadences and offbeat assertions associated with generative AI. (A detection tool backed me up on that suspicion, though Mody denies using AI to write the book.) Read: "True trends always answer a need" "White walls, neutral furniture, and barely-there decor dominated Instagram feeds and Pinterest boards. But let's be honest – minimalism isn't for everyone. It's a look, not a feeling. Dopamine design flips the script. It's not about following rules or trends. It's about creating a home that celebrates your quirks, your story, and your joy." Let me pause here to raise an eyebrow at the description of minimalism as "a look, not a feeling". Even its haters describe it as cold, which is most certainly a feeling. I also object to the use of the color white as a straw man. For every white-paint-loving minimalist like, say, John Pawson , there has always been a Barbie with a hot-pink dream house. Dopamine decor is said to have influenced the look of food packaging in real life Let me add that I met Mody in person a few years ago, while she was exhibiting a checkerboard-patterned kitchen with cabinet pulls that looked like carrots, and found her very nice. It is not my intention to whimsy-shame anyone. But given the commoditization of health in everything from peptides to bathing culture, I find it icky to glibly invoke brain chemistry in the marketing of style. Dopamine decor claims to celebrate individuality, though it's driven by repetitive social media images. It is aimed at adults, though its tutti-frutti, cutesy-naive examples look incontrovertibly juvenile. It purports to stimulate happy brain chemicals, at a time when, in the US, public health movements are being eviscerated by deranged officials. "'Dopamine decor' can boost your mood," the Washington Post declared last year , like a snake-oil salesman. Well, so can a bucket of tiramisu, until the sugar high lets you down. Read: "What to do with the TV is among the most challenging design problems in today's American home" The most disingenuous thing about this trend is the pretense that images on a screen or in a book represent plausible experience. The photos are filtered, cropped and disjointed. They whiz by, just like an endorphin rush. Dopamine decor is said to have influenced the look of food packaging in real life, but food packages are quickly thrown away. What are the long-term effects of living with frenetic decorating choices? Do they lose their happy juice over time? Do they get on one's nerves? Do they drive one insane? Yes, said Ashley Couto, who wrote an article for Business Insider magazine last year with the headline: "I redid my space with color and 'dopamine decor' designed to bring me joy. It worked at first, but I already hate it." A style touted as authentic and livable can't seem to shed its performative, Instagram-y nature This would not surprise Andréa de Paiva, a Brazilian architect who specializes in the relationship between neuroscience and building design. In a cautionary article about dopamine decor on the website of her organization, NeuroAU, she writes: "Instead of thoughtfully enhancing the environment to support well-being, these spaces risk overwhelming the senses, potentially leading to fatigue, distraction, or even stress rather than joy and motivation." De Paiva urges designers to be responsible with terminology, especially when it comes to applied science: "Titles like Dopamine Design or even NeuroArchitecture can be intriguing and marketable, but they should not be used as buzzwords to sell incomplete or oversimplified ideas." Still, you don't need to be a brain surgeon to recognize that a style touted as authentic and livable can't seem to shed its performative, Instagram-y nature. According to Marianne Plaisance , a graphic designer and photographer featured in Modi's book, some of her YouTube followers thought her space looked AI-generated. She took it as a compliment. Julie Lasky is New York-based a journalist and critic specialising in design, architecture and urbanism. She was previously deputy editor of The New York Times' weekly Home and Garden section, the editor of Change Observer, editor-in-chief of ID magazine and editor of Interiors magazine. She is also a part-time assistant professor at Parsons School of Design. The image is a screengrab taken from Instagram. Dezeen In Depth If you enjoy reading Dezeen's interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth . Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines. The post "I find it icky to glibly invoke brain chemistry in the marketing of style" appeared first on Dezeen .

pending.title: Building Tactile UX: Honoring Intentional Design With Lottie
pending.summary: When tasked with building a highly interactive, tactile web experience, the architecture must serve the art direction. In this article, Alexey Kopytin explains their architectural rationale for building a digital stress-relief squeeze toy game using Lottie animations, DOM events, and distance-based math to maintain absolute control over their designers’ intentional motion.
