pending.title: Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature
pending.summary: Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable. Accessibility as an operational capability rather than a compliance checklist or end-of-project audit, and what that looks like in practice.

content.source_text: This article is a sponsored by Level Access We know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a <div> with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working. That gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable. Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem. This is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice. The Audit Trap For years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into. Audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR , you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well. But audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple new features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way. The WebAIM Million report , which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and 'vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds. Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose. The AI Problem Nobody Wants To Name With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies. Start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you "fully give in to the vibes" and "forget that the code even exists". You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated. Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And <div onClick> is fewer tokens than <button aria-expanded="true" ...> , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path. Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern . A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”. Now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The issue wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification. The same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it. The fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails. Velocity and Accessibility Are Not Enemies This is usually where someone says, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.” In practice, the opposite tends to be true. Shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility issue caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project. Catching an accessibility issue as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented. Teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work. What Enterprise-Ready Actually Looks Like The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems . The highest-leverage place to start is the design system . One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point. Accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson. From there, it moves into the engineering workflow : Accessibility requirements are included in the Definition of Done. Pull request reviews include explicit accessibility checks. Interactive controls use semantic elements ( <button> , <a> ) by default. Keyboard navigation and focus management are treated as standard engineering concerns, not optional polish. Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation : eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y catches common issues before code is committed. LevelCI , Pa11y , and similar tools provide automated testing in CI/CD pipelines. @storybook/addon-a11y surfaces issues during component development. At that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform. Patterns That Actually Scale A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well. Constrain AI Before It Generates Instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts. Stop Hand-Rolling Complex Widgets Comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives. Capture Accessibility During Design Handoff Focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later. None of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility. The Broader Business Impact Engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction. Legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the company is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators. But compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500 . In the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million users with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor. There is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report , 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it. Step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, expos

content.source_text: 9월 17일부터 20일까지 일본 지바현 마쿠하리 멧세(Makuhari Messe)에서 열린 도쿄게임쇼 2026(Tokyo Game Show 2026, TGS). 글로벌 게임 기업 엔씨 부스는 게임 속 캐릭터를 눈앞에서 만나는 듯한 경험을 하려는 관람객들의 발길이 이어졌다. 그 중심에는 게임의 세계관을 화면 밖으로 확장한 삼성전자의 무안경 3D 디스플레이 ‘스페이셜 사이니지(Spatial Signage)’가 있었다. 이번 행사에서 엔씨가 선보인 ‘아스트라에 오라티오(Astrae Oratio)’는 마법이 일상에 스며든 판타지 세계를 배경으로 한 신전기 서브컬처 RPG다. 삼성 스페이셜 사이니지는 독자적인 ‘3D 플레이트(3D Plate)’ 기술을 적용해 별도의 3D 안경 없이도 콘텐츠에 생생한 입체감을 선사하며, 게임 속 캐릭터와 세계관을 오프라인 전시 공간으로 확장했다. 팬덤 경험 확장… 캐릭터와의 만남을 현실 공간으로 게임 퍼블리셔와 콘텐츠 IP(Intellectual Property, 지식재산권) 보유 기업에게 오프라인 공간은 디지털 콘텐츠를 현실로 가져오는 중요한 접점이다. 엔씨는 도쿄게임쇼에서 85형과 32형 스페이셜 사이니지를 부스 입구와 대기 공간 등에 배치해 관람객이 이동하는 과정에서도 게임 속 캐릭터와 세계관을 자연스럽게 경험하도록 했다. 부스 입구에는 85형 스페이셜 사이니지로 ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 게임의 주요 배경인 ‘특구청’ 건물 내 엘리베이터를 재현했다. 대형 디스플레이를 통해 캐릭터를 실제 사람과 가까운 크기로 표현해, 마치 게임 속 등장인물들이 현실 세계에 인사를 건네는 듯한 장면을 연출했다. ▲ ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 부스 입구에 설치한 85형 스페이셜 사이니지는 게임 속 다양한 캐릭터가 눈 앞으로 다가오는 듯한 연출로 관람객의 이목을 끌었다. 엔씨 아스트라에 오라티오 사업실 이용수 실장은 “관람객들이 부스에 들어서는 순간부터 실제 크기의 캐릭터와 마주하고 게임 세계에 몰입하길 바랐다”면서 “서브컬처 장르에서는 캐릭터의 생동감과 현실감이 특히 중요한데, 스페이셜 사이니지가 이런 특성을 관람객에게 효과적으로 전달할 수 있다고 판단했다”고 말했다. 현장을 찾은 관람객들은 스페이셜 사이니지가 구현한 캐릭터의 크기와 입체감에 주목했다. 콘텐츠 크리에이터 카와이 코코(Kawaii CoCo) 씨는 “캐릭터가 실제로 움직이며 상호작용하는 것처럼 생생하게 느껴졌다”며 “일반 디스플레이보다 훨씬 눈에 띄고 소셜미디어에서도 근사하게 보일 것 같아, 이 장면을 촬영해 제 구독자들에게 소개하고 싶다”고 말했다. ▲ 콘텐츠 크리에이터 카와이 코코 씨는 캐릭터의 움직임이 스페이셜 사이니지를 통해 생동감 있게 전달되어 아스트라에 오라티오 부스로 눈길이 갔다고 말했다. 스페이셜 사이니지는 52mm 1 의 얇은 두께에도 불구하고 마치 화면 뒤에 별도의 공간이 있는 듯한 깊이감을 구현한 것이 특징이다. 이러한 경험은 대중에게 게임과 캐릭터의 첫인상을 전달하는 데도 효과적으로 활용될 수 있다. 관람객 다니엘 아세로(Daniel Acero) 씨는 “처음 봤을 때 스크린 화면인 줄 전혀 몰랐고, 투명한 설치물이라고 생각했다”면서 “마치 화면 뒤에 실제 공간이 있는 것처럼 깊이감이 느껴져서 놀라웠고, 이러한 방식으로 게임 캐릭터를 소개하면 게임에 대한 관심을 높이고 캐릭터의 개성을 효과적으로 전달할 수 있을 것”이라고 말했다. 관람객 동선과 대기 공간에는 32형 스페이셜 사이니지가 설치돼 부스 전반으로 캐릭터 경험을 확장했다. 32형 제품은 49.4mm의 얇은 두께로 좁은 공간에도 유연하게 설치가 가능해, 게임 체험을 기다리는 관람객을 대상으로 캐릭터와 세계관에 대한 몰입도를 유지했다. 관람객 토마스 포르티에(Tomas Portier) 씨는 “대기 줄이 길었지만, 스페이셜 사이니지 화면을 보다보니 시간이 더 빨리 가는 느낌이었고 캐릭터에 대해서도 더 잘 알 수 있었다”며 “포스터나 일반 스크린에서 보여지는 화면보다 훨씬 생동감 있게 느껴졌다”고 말했다. ▲ 엔씨 부스 대기 공간에 설치된 32형 스페이셜 사이니지가 ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 캐릭터를 생동감 있게 보여주고 있다. 몰입감과 공간 활용은 높이고 설치 부담은 낮추고 리테일 매장과 전시·행사 공간을 운영할 때는 관람객의 시선을 사로잡는 시각적 효과뿐 아니라 설치 공간과 동선, 운영 효율까지 함께 고려해야 한다. 엔씨는 스페이셜 사이니지의 무안경 3D 표현과 슬림한 디자인을 활용해 제한된 공간에서도 관람객의 시선을 사로잡는 몰입 경험을 제공했다. 엔씨 이용수 실장은 “관람객 동선 설계는 굉장히 까다로운 일인데, 다행히 스페이셜 사이니지는 제품이 매우 얇아 시공과 설치과정이 수월했고 공간도 효율적으로 활용할 수 있었다”며 “덕분에 스크린 뒤편에 관람객을 위한 굿즈를 보관할 공간까지 확보할 수 있어 만족스러웠다”고 말했다. ▲ 엔씨 이용수 아스트라에 오라티오 사업실장. 슬림한 디자인은 관람객에게도 큰 인상을 남겼다. 관람객 데이비드 유세피(David Yousefi)씨는 “박스처럼 생겨서 훨씬 크고 두꺼운 제품일 거라고 생각했다”며 “두께가 얇아서 넓지 않은 공간에도 설치할 수 있다는 점이 인상적이다”고 말했다. ▲ (왼쪽부터) 관람객 데이비드 유세피 씨와 니콜라스 펠릭스 씨가 스페이셜 사이니지를 통해 구현된 ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 캐릭터의 생생한 존재감과 강렬한 깊이감을 체험하고 있다. 스페이셜 사이니지의 높은 공간 활용도와 설치 유연성은 캐릭터 IP 보유 기업이나 캐릭터 굿즈를 판매하는 매장 운영자에게도 캐릭터 경험을 현실 공간에 구현하는 새로운 방법을 제시한다. 게임 업계 종사자인 미겔 모렌(Miguel Moren) 씨는 “애니메이션 게임 캐릭터가 현실 공간에 구현되면서 상상의 세계와 현실 세계가 자연스럽게 어우러지는 점이 마음에 들었다”고 말했다. 관람객들은 이 같은 경험이 게임 전시회를 넘어 다양한 일상 공간으로 확대될 가능성에도 기대를 나타냈다. 마쓰시타 리오(Matsushita Rio) 씨는 “좋아하는 캐릭터가 바로 눈앞에서 움직이는 것을 보는 건 정말 즐거운 경험”이라며 “기다리는 동안에도 캐릭터의 생동감 있는 모습을 볼 수 있어서 좋았고, 아키하바라 같은 곳에서도 이런 경험을 할 수 있다면 무척 재미있을 것 같다”고 덧붙였다. 리테일 매장에서 스페이셜 사이니지의 가능성도 높이 평가했다. 니콜라스 펠릭스(Nicolas Felix) 씨는 “매장에서 옷을 착용한 모습을 보여주는 등 다양한 브랜딩과 상업적 목적으로 활용할 수 있을 것 같다”고 말했다. 데이비드 유세피(David Yousefi) 씨 역시 “테마파크나 제품을 매력적으로 선보이고 싶은 행사 현장에서도 매우 성공적으로 쓰일 수 있을 것”이라고 전했다. ▲ 관람객 마쓰시타 리오 씨가 대기 공간에서 만난 스페이셜 사이니지에 대한 인상을 전하고 있다. 같은 공간에서 관람객들이 등장하는 캐릭터를 사진으로 담고 있다. 도쿄게임쇼를 넘어: 스페이셜 사이니지의 무궁무진한 가능성 도쿄게임쇼 엔씨 부스에서 구현된 몰입형 전시 경험은 스페이셜 사이니지가 캐릭터 IP와 관람객을 연결하는 새로운 접점으로 활용될 수 있음을 보여줬다. 화면 속 캐릭터를 실제 공간에서 마주하는 듯한 연출은 게임의 세계관을 보다 직관적으로 전달하며 관람객의 관심을 끌었다. 실제 스페이셜 사이니지의 활용 영역은 게임 전시를 넘어 테마파크와 음악 페스티벌, 리테일 공간 등으로 확대되고 있다. 국내에서는 에버랜드 사파리월드 의 관람 대기 동선에 설치돼, 호랑이와 사자 등 야생동물이 화면 밖으로 튀어나올 듯한 장면을 연출하며 기다리는 시간을 사파리 경험의 일부로 바꿨다. 미국에서 열린 거버너스 볼 뮤직 페스티벌(Governors Ball Music Festival)에서는 85형 스페이셜 사이니지를 활용해 의류와 액세서리 등 페스티벌 굿즈를 입체적으로 선보였다. 도쿄게임쇼를 포함한 다양한 설치 사례는 스페이셜 사이니지가 시각적 임팩트와 공간 효율성, 그리고 관람객의 참여를 결합하여 디지털 콘텐츠를 현실 공간으로 끌어오는 방식을 보여준다. 삼성전자는 85형과 32형 등 다양한 제품 라인업과 슬림한 디자인을 바탕으로, 기존 상업 공간에 자연스럽게 적용할 수 있는 차세대 무안경 3D 디스플레이 경험을 새로운 공간으로 지속 확대해 나갈 계획이다. 85형 기준 ︎

content.source_text: British designer duo Isabel Gibson and Helen Chesner have filled The Conran Shop 's gallery with colourful, kinetic models for their London Design Festival exhibition, Motion Sickness. Spinning orbs, flapping wings and wheeled devices all feature in the exhibition, which marks 10 years since the founding of their London-based art and design studio, Isabel + Helen . The show explores the creative process of design duo Isabel + Helen Many of the models are prototypes, created for collaborations with brands such as Hermès and Burberry, or for installations at venues ranging from the V&A museum to the Coachella festival. The duo wanted to give insight into the creative process behind their projects, which typically centres around model-making. The gallery is filled with kinetic model prototypes "We saw it as an opportunity to showcase the behind-the-scenes of what we do and what we make," explained Gibson, as she and Chesner gave Dezeen a tour of the show. "The way we work, we usually jump to prototypes quite quickly," she said. "Because you can imagine how something will move and you can sketch it, but you need to get hands-on to see how it works in real life." Spinning orbs, flapping wings and wheeled devices all feature Movement has been a recurring theme in Isabel + Helen's work since they founded the studio in 2015, three years after graduating from Chelsea College of Arts, which is where they met. "We've had this obsession with movement and kinetic sculpture," Gibson told Dezeen. Read: Is London having a design renaissance? "Usually the movement has some form of transformation, or a reveal moment; that's something we're always interested in," added Chesner. "The way things move also affects how you see them," she continued. "You can have so many different emotions too; something can feel really joyful or quite sinister." The backdrop is a series of limited-edition motion paintings The backdrop to Motion Sickness is a series of limited-edition paintings, each depicting a colourful wheel. The designers produced these artworks with movement, using a kinetic machine they built themselves. It allows them to spin a paintbrush, forming a motif of concentric circles. Other focal points in the show include a toy train carrying half a dozen eggs, which wobble in time with one another as the device is wheeled along the table, and a series of 15 paper spheres that spin when you pull a string. One model is a toy train carrying half a dozen eggs Chesner said these projects develop through "trying stuff out and not being too precious about anything". "A lot of the time stuff doesn't work, but you have to just constantly build on it," she said. Simple labels encourage visitors to interact The exhibition also marks a decade of on-and-off collaboration between Isabel + Helen and The Conran Shop . One of the duo's first commissions was the store's LDF exhibition, A Load Of Jargon, presented in 2016 in collaboration with design website It's Nice That. "They saw us at the beginning, when we started out, so marking 10 years with them was really nice," added Chesner. It is among the first exhibitions that The Conran Shop has staged in the basement gallery of its store on London's Sloane Square, which has been the flagship since the closure of its previous locations on Fulham Road and Marylebone High Street. The exhibition was on show at The Conran Shop for LDF It comes a time of reinvention for the retailer, which was founded by Sir Terence Conran in 1973. Since 2023, it has shifted its business model to focus more on its own collections rather than selling pieces by other brands. Other recent milestones include the launch of a furniture collection with Francis Sultana , which was unveiled during last year's LDF. Motion Sickness was on show at The Conran Shop from 12 to 20 September as part of London Design Festival . See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. The photography is courtesy of The Conran Shop. The post Isabel + Helen showcase their "obsession with movement" with kinetic models at The Conran Shop appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Grinham Research Group at Harvard University has developed an insulating cladding tile made from waste wool , which was presented at this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale . In an installation named Upcycling Wool Ecologies, Grinham Research Group showcased its tiles on a timber frame in Oslo 's Sofienberg Church as part of the triennale's main exhibition, which takes place from 17 September to 1 October. Grinham Research Group saw the potential in wool's insulative, fire-resistant and antibacterial properties, and wanted to save it from being discarded as a residual material in the agricultural and textile industries. Harvard University's Grinham Research Group has developed a wall tile made from waste wool The group also wanted to develop a material that could help facilitate building reuse. Their solution was a tile with a multi-layer design that can be applied to the exterior of buildings, avoiding the costly work of digging into a wall to upgrade its insulation. Made from recycled wool, the tiles have a low-density back panel that acts as an insulating board and a denser outer panel with greater durability and weather resistance. The cladding tiles were showcased at Oslo Architecture Triennale "We need pluralistic solutions that reflect the complexity of nature," Grinham Research Group founder Jonathan Grinham told Dezeen. "Architecture can actively design these new industrial ecologies that retain the value of materials, skilled labour, and existing industries while creating scalable retrofit solutions," he continued. "By transforming waste wool into durable exterior cladding, biogenic carbon captured through grass, sheep, and wool can be retained in the built environment, while the same material improves the performance and extends the useful life of existing buildings." Read: Finnish company launches "world's most carbon-storing building material" To make the tiles, wool is treated with an alkaline solution that partially breaks down its keratin proteins, before a mechanical process further separates the material into a liquid. Citric acid is then added, which, when heated with the wool-derived keratin, binds residual and unprocessed wool fibres into a rigid composite without the need for a petrochemical resin. According to the group, around 1.95 billion kilograms of raw wool are produced each year, with approximately 60 per cent used for wool clothing manufacturing. Unused wool is typically stockpiled, burned or buried. A dense, durable layer is placed over an insulating panel "The decline of domestic textile manufacturing, competition from synthetics, and selective grading have left enormous quantities of wool without a viable market," said Grinham. "Wool has lost its economic value, but not its material properties," he continued. "We're developing new chemistries that transform this overlooked natural polymer into a useful biocomposite for building insulation and cladding." Grinham Research Group pressed the tiles into a fluted design For the Oslo Architecture Triennale installation, Grinham Research Group sourced preconsumer waste wool from the American Woolen Company in Connecticut. It used a mixture of naturally coloured and dyed fibres, which resulted in the variations in tile colours. The tiles showcased at the event featured a fluted surface design, but the material could be pressed into different shapes and designs. Other material innovations that have recently featured on Dezeen include a wall surface made from forestry industry offcuts that is almost pure carbon, and a dress made from living mycelium that can repair itself . The photography and video are courtesy of Grinham Research Group. Oslo Architecture Triennale takes place from 17 September to 1 October at Sofienberg Church in Oslo, Norway. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world. The post Harvard University transforms waste wool into cladding for retrofits appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: From hastily installed sheds and tents to more intricate structures with signage and considered design, author Penny Hardy highlights the absurdity, delight and ingenuity of dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic . Collected in Hardy's recently announced book, Pandemic Architecture: NYC Dining Sheds 2020-2024 , the sheds represent a very specific time in the landscape of the city, when restaurants tried to operate during indoor dining restrictions. Many have since been deconstructed, as the city tries to implement a standardised shed programme to keep the seating while maintaining safety and sanitation standards. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani recently cleared the legal way for year-round installation . Hardy took photos of the sheds in Downtown Manhattan on walks during the height of the pandemic and afterwards, as many remained up for years after the 2020 to 2021 lockdowns. Though many of the restaurants have since closed or moved, Hardy believes that it's clear that the impact of the structures has changed the way we view the streetscape. Penny Hardy's new book looks at the range of impromptu dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic "These structures created a new typology for building in public space and have forever changed the way we use the street," she told Dezeen. "Before this new typology, the street was aggressively preserved as a place of transit by the city. Now, in addition to transit, it offers a place for people to connect and socialise." She added that the recent city legislation opens up room for a return to the creativity that has been limited by the high costs of storage and assembly of the structures during the winter months. "The restaurant owners' resourcefulness, humour, and wildly different tastes made the streets more varied and alive," said Hardy. "The structures were raw, inventive, funny, and as varied as New York itself. They brought an old-school punk, DIY spirit back into an increasingly polished city." The book contains dozens of examples taken by Hardy, as well as essays by New York writers such as Michael Bullock and Fred Bernstein . Read on for a selection of images from the book and Hardy's commentary. "Suburban design via Home Depot" in Greenwich Village "'We need to get something up quick. Go to Home Depot. Improvise'. I imagine this was the directive given to an employee or self-imposed by the owner. "Ubiquitous 'colonial moulded interior door' with handle and lock, surrounded by vibrant magenta plastic panelling, taped heart detailing and painted soft pink plywood. Why didn’t they paint the door?" "Less is enough" in West Village "Use structures that already exist. They provide privacy, protection, and shelter from the weather. Why make things more complicated? "The neighbourhood institution, Julius, kept it simple. Perhaps the owner was a camper – bring in a tent from the country, order a few more, and they were done." "Learning from Las Vegas" in Little Italy "If only Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown had been able to see these sheds: one a decorated shed, the other architecture becoming the sign itself. "Baby John created a dining structure fit for his namesake. A curved vinyl banquette pulled from deep storage, a monumental crown, and signage visible from blocks away combined to create a VIP experience that drew long lines and gave the place instant cachet. Venturi and Scott Brown would surely have joined the queue." "An imposing mash-up of classical architecture" in Little Italy "Down the street, a fellow, longtime restaurateur created an imposing mash-up of classical architecture and gothic detailing. "Its sense of grandeur, in direct contrast to the temporality of the sheds, creates a playful contradiction. Venturi and Brown would have appreciated the 'complexity and contradiction'." "The wild west" in Chinatown "Almost overnight, the street became a space of radical improvisation, where rigid building restrictions of the city were tossed aside, as restaurants fought for survival. "Exposed electrical wires brought air conditioners and fans into the sheds. Practical and terrifying at the same time." "Take me away" in SoHo "Perhaps we can transport them somewhere tropical, offering a brief respite from the city. If they can't get on an aeroplane, maybe the dining shed can take them there. "A thatched roof, white curtains tied with rope tassels, and tropical plants conjure a beachfront cabana." "Co-existing" in West Village "The interweaving of street signs and structures with the dining sheds created humorous juxtapositions. "Why extend the structure to enclose the postal relay box? Rather than stopping short of it, the shed carefully absorbs it into the design, even carving out space for the neighbouring tree. Existing street infrastructure becomes part of the architecture." "Living in the street" in NoHo "Owners looked for ways to make street dining feel comfortable, creating environments that helped diners forget they were sitting in a place never meant for a meal. "The dark-stained wood panelling and curated selection of framed paintings evoke the atmosphere of farm life, creating the feeling of dining in the countryside." "Architecture, design and construction professionals enter the fray" in Flatiron "Whether these were designed by an architect, interior designer or contractor, they all had the visible sign of a professional being involved. Material choices, lighting, and built-in seating suggest a level of planning beyond improvisation. "A classic gable roof, clapboard siding, and exposed stud framing suggest the work of a general contractor with spare materials from their last project?" "Even the heaters have been carefully considered" in Nolita "The minimal, modular design suggests the involvement of an architect. "Even the heaters have been carefully considered, integrated beneath the seating." The post Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: The sandy tones of Belgium's North Sea shore informed the interiors of this penthouse , designed by Antwerp-based studio Merckx-Holvoet Architecten. The holiday home, named V Penthouse, occupies the ninth and tenth floors of a building in Duinbergen, a seaside village in the West Flanders region of Belgium. Merckx-Holvoet Architecten has completed a penthouse in Belgium "[We] aimed for an interior that envelops without overwhelming, one that reveals itself slowly rather than all at once," Merckx-Holvoet Architecten co-founders Marc Merckx and Sebastien Holvoet told Dezeen. "The design centres on poetry and refinement, built around a reduced palette of materials and colours," the architects continued. Merckx-Holvoet Architecten filled the 150-square-metre penthouse with a pared-back material palette and neutral tones that echo the dunes of the beach it overlooks. "The starting point was the sand colour found along the coastline," project architect Jef De Saedeleer said. "Where the view stretches out over the sea, the material palette echoes this seamlessly." Sandy tones inform the interior scheme Throughout the residence, walls covered in sandblasted Travertino Noce stone are teamed with lime-based flooring and solid oakwood details. Across both floors, the penthouse follows a simple, rectangular layout, with an entrance foyer at the centre of the lower floor where Merckx-Holvoet Architecten installed a sculptural, solid oak staircase leading upstairs. V Penthouse features a pared-back material palette The foyer is flanked by a sea-view living room on one side and a kitchen-cum-dining area on the other – both opening into a verandah. The studio chose neutral-hued furnishings for the living room, which it paired with tactile, modernist furniture pieces including a coffee table clad in parchment leather. Read: Woonpioniers builds a house that "moves with the dunes" Floor-to-ceiling Travertino Noce shutters conceal built-in worktops and storage in the kitchen, complemented by an oak wood island topped with a chamfered block of Egyptian sandstone. Merckx-Holvoet Architecten custom-made an Italian lavastone-topped table and an L-shaped bench crafted with Egyptian sandstone and oak wood for the dining area. The studio also sourced woven dining chairs for this space. A solid oak staircase connects the two levels The homogeneous material palette continues in the primary bedroom and guest suites located upstairs. The primary bedroom features an ensuite topped with a sloping roof. Here, Merckx-Holvoet Architecten installed picture windows by the bathtub as well as the shower area, both providing endless views of the North Sea. Much of the furniture and lighting was custom-made by Merckx-Holvoet Architecten, including a mahogany table lamp and an outdoor aluminium stool for the verandah. Minimalist artwork is dotted across the walls, including pieces by artists Andy Warhol and Sol Lewitt. Picture windows provide endless views of the North Sea Merckx-Holvoet Architecten is an architecture and design practice founded in 2018 by Merckx and Holvoet. Elsewhere in Belgium, Atelier Vens Vanbelle referenced brick industrial buildings to create a family home and Studio Okami Architecten extended a residence by adding a pavilion-like volume clad in green marble . The photography is by Eric Petschek . The post Merckx-Holvoet Architecten designs seaside penthouse to evoke North Sea coast appeared first on Dezeen .

content.source_text: Architecture collective Badweather has transformed a 17-metre canal boat into Soak, an off-grid bathhouse that moves to a new location along London 's waterways every two weeks. Soak combines a wood-fired sauna , two cold plunge pools, showers, changing facilities and a small bar for up to 12 people. Soak is housed in a restored 56-foot widebeam canal boat It operates without mains water, electricity or sewage connections, instead drawing water directly from the canal and passing it through a six-stage filtration and UV treatment system before it is used for bathing. Electricity is generated by solar panels and stored in an onboard battery system, while a wood-fired stove provides heat for the sauna. The sauna is lined with timber and features a wood-burning stove The project was developed by Badweather co-founder Leo Sixsmith and chef and former restaurateur Riccardo Codacci-Pisanelli, who wanted to create a communal bathing space that could move through the city rather than occupy a permanent site. "The changing location of the boat means that the view through these windows is never the same," Sixsmith told Dezeen. Circular portholes bring views of the canalside vegetation into the sauna Soak began with a near-derelict 20-year-old canal boat, with rotten floors, water damage and a steel hull that required extensive restoration. Around 40 people worked on its conversion, with the existing hull dictating much of the interior layout. The exterior was painted cream with black and red detailing, while circular portholes puncture the sides of the boat. Read: Future Simple Studio creates "contemporary vocabulary" for Montreal bathhouse Inside, the original 11-inch openings have been enlarged to 18 and 32 inches, with fiery-red frames that make the windows stand out against the hull. At the bow, a large picture window replaces an original steel door, opening the narrow interior towards the water. Blue steps lead from the changing area towards the plunge room The interior follows the boat's long, narrow form. Visitors enter through a dark changing and reception area lined with stained marine plywood. They then pass into a brighter plunge and shower room, featuring pale green tiles, stainless-steel pools and a central skylight that brings daylight into the boat. "The wet room is intentionally kept completely free of timber," Sixsmith said. "Its harder, clinical finish allows for easier maintenance, while heightening the sensory contrast with the warmth of the sauna." Stainless-steel plunge pools sit beneath a central skylight in the wet room At the bow, the sauna is lined with thermally treated Aspen and Alder wood and is centred around a wood-burning stove. Two benches were suspended from aluminium beams rather than supported by legs, allowing them to overlap within the tapered hull. A large window frames the canal from one of the plunge pools The boat's cramped dimensions were a major constraint, but Badweather aimed to use them to shape the interior. "Every centimetre had to work exceptionally hard," Sixsmith said. Founded in London in 2019 by Oli Brenner, Sophie Mei Birkin and Sixsmith, Badweather is an experimental architecture, scenography and design collective working across installations, objects, lighting and buildings. A large window opens the sauna towards the surrounding canal landscape Its previous work includes temporary structures for nightclubs and festivals, including the ongoing Pipeline project, a floating communal hearth made from reused corrugated polycarbonate. Other bathhouses featured on Dezeen include a communal sauna and hydrotherapy bathhouse in Montreal and the turquoise-tiled Komaeyu public bathhouse in the suburbs of Tokyo. The photography is by Kaye Song. The post Badweather converts derelict canal boat into London's first off-grid bathhouse appeared first on Dezeen .
content.original_title: Badweather converts derelict canal boat into London's first off-grid bathhouse

content.source_text: Meet Meta VR Glasses: our most advanced device yet, delivering a personal cinema, courtside seat, workspace, and gaming console, all in a pair of glasses that weighs about 100 grams — roughly the same as a deck of cards. Thanks to the breakthrough glasses form factor, there are no straps or heavy hardware on your face. The open sides and passthrough camera keep you aware of what’s happening nearby. You can wear Meta VR Glasses to comfortably watch a full movie or privately work on a long flight while maintaining a sense of the world around you. Designed for Comfort, Clarity, and Power Meta VR Glasses are five times lighter than Meta Quest 3, primarily because of their two-part system. The VR Glasses handle the sensors and display, while the puck, connected by an optical tether, handles compute, battery, and storage, and conveniently clips to your pocket or bag. Meta VR Glasses feature 5K Infinite Display built on micro-OLED panels, with 37 pixels per degree, delivering stunning clarity and detail — great for text legibility. The ultra-compact pancake lenses built specifically for this device are the reason cinema-grade clarity can live in something that looks like glasses. With Dolby Vision, you’ll see every scene come alive with ultra-vivid color, sharp contrast, and lifelike detail, and Dolby Atmos spatial audio is integrated directly into the frames. We’ve integrated your Meta AI agent directly into the operating system. You can just talk to Meta VR Glasses or use your eyes and natural hand gestures to do things like play a movie, open an app, adjust your workspace, or search for whatever you’re looking for. No controllers needed. Meta VR Glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, enabling an exceptionally high-performance experience, fast load times, and breakthrough efficiency. The puck battery delivers up to three hours of continuous high-resolution media playback and supports 45W fast charging. Your Own Immersive Theater and Courtside Seat Meta VR Glasses are the first ever IMAX Enhanced certified VR device and will be one of the only ways to experience select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio at home. In November, Disney+ subscribers can start streaming movies like Marvel’s The Avengers, Marvel Studios’ Black Panther , and more in 3D in select countries, with immersive themed viewing environments like Tatooine, Avengers Tower, and Scare Floor. You’ll also be able to watch VR Enhanced versions of iconic films like Avengers: Infinity War and Star Wars: A New Hope in the new Disney Immersive Cinema by ILM app. Your surroundings will be transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio to feel like you’re not just watching a scene, but living inside it. We’re working with Prime Video , YouTube , DIRECTV , AMC+ , Crunchyroll , Plex , ESPN , Tubi, and more to provide the best media lineup of any VR device. Peacock , HBO Max, and Paramount+ are also offering their 3D media catalogs for the very first time. The library will keep growing, with thousands of titles available internationally by Meta VR Glasses’ launch, including 3D favorites from Lionsgate. We’re also partnering with director James Cameron and Lightstorm Vision to debut “first time in 3D” blockbusters in 2027. We’ve also worked with ESPN to give you “Immersive Sports” with a front-row seat, 8K streaming, and 180-degree views, starting with college football this year on Meta Quest and more sports to come in 2027. Once Meta VR Glasses launch, we’ll have over 100 immersive live sports events to watch each year from the best seat in the house, thanks to our partners at MLB, NBC Sports, TNT Sports, and UFC. This is just the beginning, with new 3D movies releasing every month, new immersive sporting events available throughout the year, and new partner experiences dropping regularly. Your Office, Wherever You Are Meta VR Glasses give you a massive screen — or several if you want — anywhere you are, creating a personalized, private place to work. Turn any flat surface into a keyboard and touchpad, so you can type out a reply without carrying extra hardware. And with full-color passthrough, you can still see your desk, mobile phone, and surroundings while you work. https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/05_VRGlasses_inline_cafe.mp4 For gaming, there will be more than 75 games at launch that you can play solely with hand gestures, and with XBOX Cloud Gaming, you can stream hundreds more. Introducing Hologram Calling Lastly, we’re introducing hologram technology to provide a photorealistic digital version of you, including your real-time expressions and reactions, for hands-free video calling on Meta VR Glasses. When you see someone’s hologram in Meta VR Glasses, they appear in front of you with spatial audio placing their voice where they are, so it feels like you’re in the same room. If others are joining the call from a mobile phone or computer, they see your hologram on their screen as well. It works with whichever calling app you’re using, from WhatsApp to Zoom. https://about.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/06_VRGlasses_inline_hologram.mp4 Coming Spring 2027 Meta VR Glasses will go on sale Spring 2027 for $1,299.99 USD. The post Introducing Meta VR Glasses: A Cinema, Courtside Seat, and Workspace in Just 100 Grams appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

content.source_text: Chinese interior designer Bin Wu 's book Timeless East explores the idea of a design language rooted in the philosophical context of the East. For this roundup, he picks six of his own favourite projects in China and abroad. The Design Language of Timeless East features 17 projects completed by Wu and his studio W Design , spanning interior design, art installations and design research. Wu's aim was to challenge the absence of Eastern voices from modern design narratives. Instead, he hoped to show Eastern design through a different lens that would be more true to its original roots and promote a spiritual connection. The new book features 17 projects completed by Bin Wu and his studio W Design "Whether it was the Japonisme of the nineteenth century or the Chinoiserie of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, these were projections of the Eastern imagination filtered through a Western lens – not distillations of Eastern culture and art articulated by the East itself," Wu told Dezeen. "Even in the wake of China's rapid economic ascent over the past two decades, this predicament remains unresolved," he continued. "The Design Language of Timeless East is a response issued from the Eastern subject itself." Here, Dezeen selects six projects from the book that explore the Timeless East design language: Photo by Wang Ting Hai Shang restaurant, Shanghai, 2023 At this fusion restaurant in Shanghai , Wu combined raw materials with a dark colour palette to create a subtle atmosphere with a mysterious feel. Sea reeds are stacked into a circular enclosure at the entrance, which leads to a narrow corridor paved with rustic stone. This was designed to be reminiscent of old Chinese water towns – historic towns known for their bridges and rivers – and opens up to an open kitchen. The studio kept the exposed beams to reveal the history of the building, while adding a countertop crafted from a massive ink stone. Photo by Wang Ting The Fame, Chengdu, 2024 Wu designed this visitor centre for a residential complex in Chengdu , using locally sourced materials to evoke the experience of wandering in a garden. The entrance hall was clad with bamboo strips that allow light to filter through the gaps, creating a constantly shifting interplay of light and shadow. Connecting corridors weave together various open spaces, creating a fluid and ever-changing atmosphere that aligns with the Chinese garden principle of "not revealing everything at once". The main social space features dark terracotta panels on the wall that were designed to resemble local roof tiles in a nod to the rustic mountain dwellings nearby. Photo by Wang Ting Deqin Meri Poodom Hotel, Deqin, 2024 Located at the foot of Meri Snow Mountain, a sacred place for the local Tibetan community, this hotel design aims to balance spirituality and everyday living. Wu designed its central staircase to evoke a white pagoda – a historic building of religious significance. He created its encased and overlapping stairs, each turning at a forty-five-degree angle, for visitors to feel like they are climbing towards the sky. Locally relevant objects were incorporated into the interiors, including yak bells and black pottery. All guest rooms frame part of the Meri Mountain, which has 13 sacred peaks in total, to make visitors feel closer to the heart of Tibetan faith. Photo by Zheng Hao Collector's Mansion, Shanghai, 2024 W Design completed the facade renovation, as well as a display apartment, for this luxury residential complex in Shanghai's former French Concession. Orderly arranged balconies add a sense of rhythm to the otherwise clean, minimalist facade. Inside the apartment, the living room opens up after a narrow foyer. The interiors have a restrained colour and material palette to create a tranquil atmosphere and include tactile furniture with rough surfaces designed to resemble old objects. Photo by Shi Dai Pan Yuan: Momentality Unfold, Milan, 2024 Wu revealed this paper installation during Milan Design Week 2024. Located in the central courtyard of the Cortile d'Onore at the University of Milan, the installation reflected the Eastern architectural emphasis on change, seeking eternity within impermanence. Based on the theme "momentality", it used large-scale paper scrolls, a material commonly found in Eastern architecture and painting, to form an Eastern garden experience that contrasted the surrounding historical architecture. The installation was made from lightweight and durable DuPont Tyvek paper, which has a texture that strongly resembles traditional Eastern Xuan paper. Photo by Zhu Di Arbour, Shanghai, 2025 W Design created a quietly elegant "indoor theatre" for this residence in Shanghai, where soft lighting, a spiral staircase, and refined vintage furnishings evoke a sense of nostalgia. Drapes were used across dining rooms and bedrooms to soften the spatial boundaries, while wood furniture and timber flooring add warmth to the space. content.source_text: Dezeen has announced the 50 projects featured in the Top 50: Europe, Middle East and Africa list as part of the Regional Showcases for Dezeen Awards 2026 . Launched as a new initiative for the 2026 edition of the awards programme , each Top 50 list celebrates the best projects in three regions globally: Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA), Asia Pacific (APAC) and the Americas. The projects in the Regional Showcases have been selected by Dezeen's editors. Each Top 50 list highlights both the variety of creative excellence and the nuanced differences in output across the 91 countries that entered Dezeen Awards this year. This year's Top 50: EMEA list features projects spanning architecture, interiors and design, from countries including Italy , Lebanon and Rwanda , as well as France , South Africa and Turkey . Dezeen Awards 2026 Regional Showcases revealed this week Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble , will reveal all projects featured in the Regional Showcases this week. The APAC list will be published tomorrow, followed by the Americas list on Friday. This year's Dezeen Awards 2026 shortlists, selected by our world-renowned judges , will be announced on Dezeen between 21 and 23 September. The Top 50: EMEA list is below, with each project linked to a dedicated page on the Dezeen Awards website, where you can find an image and more information about the project. Join us and our Dezeen Awards judges at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November to find out this year's winners. The special occasion is the perfect opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work. content.source_text: 글. 박이슬(스노우) / 공통플랫폼개발팀 안녕하세요, 여기어때컴퍼니 공통플랫폼개발팀 스노우입니다. 1편 에서는 Confluence와 Jira에 흩어진 문서를 모아 검색 가능한 형태로 바꿨고, 2편에서는 그 위에 LightRAG와 Navigator를 얹었습니다. 여기까지 오면 질문을 던졌을 때 답이 돌아옵니다. 그런데 만들고 나서 가장 오래 붙잡고 있었던 건 검색이 아니었습니다. 만든 것이 제대로 동작하는지 확인하는 일이었습니다. 이번 편은 그 이야기입니다. 질의를 던졌을 때 무엇이 오갔는지 보이게 만들고, 그게 맞는 답인지 채점하고, 그렇게 검증한 검색을 에이전트가 쓸 수 있게 내보내기까지. 그리고 마지막에는 그렇게 만든 도구가 지금 어디에서 어떻게 쓰이고 있는지까지의 이야기입니다. LLM Observability와 LLM 평가하기 LLM과 RAG는 잘 돌아가고 있는지 눈으로 확인하기 어려운 시스템입니다. LLM의 입출력은 자연어이다 보니, 지금 모델이 좋은 답변을 했는지 못했는지를 판단하기가 굉장히 어렵습니다. 답이 그럴듯하면 맞아 보입니다. 근거 문서들을 함께 돌려주니 더 그래 보입니다. 실제로는 엉뚱한 문서를 집어왔는데도 모델이 매끄럽게 문장을 만들어내면, 읽는 사람은 그걸 알아차리기가 어렵습니다. 비용도 마찬가지입니다. 문서 하나를 처리하는 데 LLM 호출이 몇 번이나 붙는지, 그게 한 달에 얼마가 되는지는 청구서가 오기 전까지 알 수 없습니다. 이런 문제점을 해결해주는 도구로써 최근에 LLM에 특화된 APM(Application Performance Monitoring)들이 나왔습니다. 그 중 저희는 Langfuse 를 선택했습니다. LLM 애플리케이션에 특화된 오픈소스 관측 플랫폼으로, 요청 하나가 어떤 경로를 거쳤는지를 trace 단위로 기록하고 보여주는 모니터링 툴입니다. Langfuse trace 추적 예시 일반적인 APM과 다른 점은, 프롬프트와 응답 전문, 사용 토큰, 모델별 단가에 따른 비용이 호출마다 남는다는 점입니다. 검색 → 프롬프트 조립 → 생성으로 이어지는 여러 단계를 하나의 trace로 묶어 보여주기 때문에, 어느 단계에서 시간이 걸렸고 어디서 토큰이 나갔는지를 한 화면에서 확인할 수 있습니다. RAG 평가 파이프라인 구축 Langfuse를 붙이면서 어디에 시간과 비용이 나가는지 보이게 됐습니다. 다만 검색 결과가 좋은지 나쁜지는 여전히 알 수 없었습니다. trace에 남는 건 무엇이 오갔는지, 그게 맞는 답인지가 아니기 때문입니다. Langfuse에는 Experiment 라는 이름으로 해당 기능을 지원하고 있습니다. 데이터셋을 만들고, 평가체계를 구축하고, 실험을 돌려 결과를 남기는 것까지 하나의 플랫폼 안에서 가능합니다. 이번 프로젝트에서는 이 기능을 최대한 활용하였습니다. 무엇을 물어볼 것인가 RAG 시스템을 평가하기 위해선, 먼저 평가대상인 질문-답변 쌍을 제작해야했습니다. 검색이 실패하는 방식은 하나가 아니기 때문에 먼저 사내 지식을 기반으로 답변할 수 있는 질문 유형을 일곱 가지로 나누고, 유형별로 질문과 정답 쌍을 작성했습니다. 유형을 나눠서 데이터셋을 생성한다면, 평가 이후 어디가 약한지가 점수와 함께 드러날 것이라고 생각했습니다. 검색이 제대로 됐는가 질문셋이 준비됐으니 이제 확인할 차례입니다. RAG에서 답이 틀리는 경로는 크게 둘인데, 애초에 엉뚱한 문서를 가져왔거나 문서는 맞는데 모델이 잘못 읽은 경우입니다 앞쪽은 정보 검색 분야에서 오래 쓰인 지표들로 확인할 수 있습니다. Recall@5 : 정답 문서가 상위 5개 안에 들어왔는가 Hit Rate : 정답 문서를 한 번이라도 회수했는가 MRR : 정답 문서가 몇 번째로 올라왔는가 질문마다 정답 문서를 지정해뒀기 때문에 리트리버가 돌려준 목록과 대조하면 자동으로 계산됩니다. Langfuse Python SDK로 데이터셋을 불러와 실험을 돌리고, 이 지표들을 계산하는 evaluator를 붙였습니다. LLM을 거치지 않으니 빠르고, 같은 입력에는 항상 같은 값이 나옵니다. 그래서 답은 좋아졌는가 (LLM-as-a-judge) 다만 이 지표들이 좋아진다고 최종 답변이 좋아진다는 보장은 없습니다. 정답 문서를 1등으로 가져와도 모델이 엉뚱한 문단을 인용할 수 있고, 반대로 순위가 낮아도 Agent가 검색을 몇 번 더 해서 결국 답을 찾아낼 수도 있습니다. 저희가 최종적으로 만드는 건 Agent가 쓰는 도구이니, 최종적으로 확인해야 할 건 그 도구를 쓴 Agent의 답변입니다. LLM as a judge 동작 과정 그래서 MCP를 붙인 Agent를 하나 만들어 답변까지 생성하게 했습니다. 남은 문제는 채점입니다. 답변이 자연어라 맞았는지 틀렸는지를 문자열 비교로 가를 수 없고, 그렇다고 실험할 때마다 사람이 수십 건을 읽어 점수를 매길 수도 없습니다. 채점은 답변을 만든 모델과 분리된 LLM에게 맡겼습니다. 이를 LLM-as-a-judge 라고 합니다. 미리 작성해둔 정답과 실제 응답을 함께 넘겨 0에서 1 사이의 “ 정확도 ” 점수를 매기게 했습니다. 정답을 함께 주는 게 중요합니다. 심판이 혼자 판단하는 게 아니라 정답표를 들고 채점하는 셈이라, 점수가 덜 흔들립니다. 평가 파이프라인을 정리하면 두 층으로 측정을 합니다. 검색 지표는 리트리버가 옳은 문서를 가져왔는지를 보고, LLM-as-a-Judge는 그 문서로 만든 답이 실제로 답변이 되는지를 확인합니다. 답이 틀렸을 때 검색이 문제였는지 생성이 문제였는지, 두 층을 비교하면 가려집니다. 프로젝트의 모든 변경은 이 평가 파이프라인을 통과합니다. 프롬프트에서 문장 하나를 지우든 툴의 파라미터를 바꾸든, 먼저 실험을 돌려 점수를 보고 수정 사항을 적용할지를 정했습니다. 실험은 한 번으로 끝내지 않고 보통 3회 이상 반복해 평균을 냈습니다. LLM 응답에는 편차가 있어서, 한 번의 결과로는 개선인지 운인지 구분할 수 없기 때문입니다. Run마다 정확도와 함께 지연시간·토큰·비용이 같이 남기 때문에, “정확도는 그대로인데 토큰만 줄었다”처럼 한 축만 움직인 변경도 그대로 보였습니다. MCP 서빙 남은 건 지금까지 준비한걸 어떻게 Agent에게 제공하느냐입니다. MCP 서빙 도구로는 FastMCP 를 택했습니다. Python으로 MCP 서버를 만들 때 사실상 표준처럼 쓰이고 있고, 데코레이터 하나로 함수 시그니처와 타입 힌트에서 툴 스키마를 자동으로 만들어줍니다. 저희처럼 툴 명세(docstring과 파라미터 설명)를 자주 고치는 상황에서는, 명세가 코드 옆에 붙어 있어 함께 관리된다는 점이 특히 편했습니다. transport 방식은 HTTP Streamable을 골랐습니다. LLM 호출 권한과 LightRAG 접근 권한이 서버에만 있어야 했기 때문입니다. stdio 방식이라면 사용자 로컬에서 서버가 뜨면서 이 권한들이 함께 나가야 하는데, 그럴 수는 없었습니다. 서버를 한 곳에 두고 사내 에이전트들이 원격으로 붙는 구조가 맞았습니다. 단순하게 생각하면 MCP 서버를 띄우고 필요한 도구를 연결해주는 것으로 서빙은 끝이라고 생각할 수 있지만, 생각보다 고려할 점이 많았습니다. MCP는 툴 정의와 명세만 주어지기 때문에, 그걸 어떻게 사용할지는 온전히 에이전트의 자유입니다. 의도한 동작 흐름이 있어도 에이전트가 이를 무시하면 기대보다 못한 결과가 나올 수 있습니다. 저희 MCP는 크게 세 가지 동작을 제공합니다. 의미 기반으로 chunk 가져오기 (get_lightrag_kg) 특정 요소의 주변 관계망 탐색하기 (get_page_hierarchy / get_issue_hierarchy) 특정 요소의 실제 내용 읽기 (read_confluence_page / read_jira_issue) 저희가 의도한 건 1 → 2 → 3을 유기적으로 오가며 답변에 필요한 근거를 에이전틱하게 모으는 흐름이었습니다. 그런데 처음에는 1을 한 번 호출하고 바로 답을 만들어버렸습니다. 청크 몇 개로 그럴듯하게 답변을 하지만, 2편에서 이야기한 “문서가 어디에 놓여 있는가”는 전혀 쓰이지 않는 상태였고 기대보다 아쉬운 답변을 생성했습니다. MCP Protocol의 Initialization Phase에서 Instructions이 전달 결국 MCP에 붙는 에이전트들에게 툴 오케스트레이션을 의도적으로 알려줄 필요가 있었고, 이를 서버 instructions 로 해결했습니다. MCP 서버는 클라이언트와 연결하는 초기화 절차에서 instructions를 함께 내려보낼 수 있고, 클라이언트는 해당 텍스트를 LLM 컨텍스트에 실어줍니다. 즉 툴 목록과 함께 “이 툴들을 이런 순서로 쓰라”는 안내가 같이 전달되는 셈입니다. 지시를 충실히 따르는 모델이라면 의도한 대로 움직이게 됩니다. ### 예시: "공통 카프카 토픽 명명 규칙이 어떻게 되나요?" 1. get_lightrag_kg(query="공통 카프카 토픽 명명 규칙") → chunks 중 path = "공통플랫폼개발팀/.../공통카프카/공통카프카 요청 가이드" 확보 2. KG가 알려준 path 하나에 만족하지 말고, 부모 경로의 hierarchy도 함께 확인 - get_page_hierarchy(path="공통플랫폼개발팀/.../공통카프카") → 같은 레벨의 형제 문서(예: "공통카프카 주의사항") 발견 3. 발견된 관련 페이지를 모아 읽기 - read_confluence_page(path="...공통카프카 요청 가이드") 4. 명명 규칙과 그 예외·제약이 출처와 함께 모두 확보되면 종료, 답변 작성 물론 다른 방법도 있습니다. MCP를 사용하는 Skill을 따로 만들어 제공할 수도 있었겠지만, MCP 쪽에서 Skill 사용을 강제할 수는 없으니 같은 문제가 반복될 수 있습니다. 그래서 instructions에 담는 방향으로 확정했습니다. 측정하고, 고치고, 다시 측정하기 서빙을 붙이고 나서 손댄 것은 리트리버가 아니라 MCP 명세였습니다. 서버 instructions와 툴 docstring, 파라미터의 형태가 에이전트가 우리 도구에 대해 아는 전부이고, 여기에 성능이 생각보다 민감하게 반응했습니다. 그래서 명세를 대상으로 프롬프트 엔지니어링을 진행했습니다. 프롬프트는 짧을수록 좋았다 가장 크게 효과를 본 건 프롬프트를 줄이는 작업이었습니다. 경량 모델을 사용할수록 긴 프롬프트의 중간부 지시를 흘리는 경향(lost in the middle) 이 강해서, 규칙을 촘촘히 적어둘수록 오히려 덜 지켰습니다. MCP instructions와 툴 docstring에서 중복된 지시들을 걷어내고 핵심만 남겼습니다. 도구 명세도 프롬프트입니다 trace를 열어보면 도구를 만든 방식 때문에 틀리는 경우가 적지 않았습니다. 도구의 이름과 설명, 파라미터 형태는 모델이 읽는 또 하나의 프롬프트입니다. 두 가지를 고쳤습니다. 한 번에 여러 개를 받던 것을 하나씩 받도록 . 문서를 읽는 도구는 원래 페이지 목록을 한꺼번에 받았습니다. 호출을 아끼는 효율적인 설계처럼 보였지만, 결과가 목록으로 돌아오면 모델은 어느 결과가 어느 요청에 대한 것인지부터 맞춰봐야 합니다. 문서를 읽기도 전에 짝을 맞추는 데 생각을 쓰는 셈입니다. 여러 개가 필요하면 도구를 여러 번 부르면 그만이라, 한 번에 하나씩만 읽도록 바꿨습니다. 사람이 읽기 좋은 값 대신 기계가 다루기 좋은 값으로 . 문서를 식별할 때 처음에는 팀/폴더/제목 같은 경로를 사용했습니다. 그런데 제목 자체에 슬래시가 들어가 있는 경우 폴더 구분과 헷갈리지 않도록 따로 특수기호로 표시해두는데, 모델이 그 표시를 오타로 보고 지워버리는 일이 생겼습니다. 한 글자 차이로 문서를 못 찾으니 빈 결과가 돌아옵니다. 이후 모델이 다듬을 여지가 없는 고유 ID로 바꿨습니다. 둘 다 검색을 건드린 수정이 아닙니다. 무엇을 어떤 모양으로 건네줄지를 바꿨을 뿐인데 정확도가 모델에 따라 3~9%p 움직였습니다. 에이전트는 우리가 준 명세만 보고 판단하니, 명세를 다듬는 일이 곧 성능을 다듬는 일이었습니다. 그리고 그 효과는 경량 모델일수록 크게 나타났습니다. 1편에서 미리 보여드린 숫자는 범용 문서 검색 MCP와 저희가 구축한 Atlas Retriever MCP를 비교한 결과입니다. 주목할 만한 건 정확도와 토큰이 함께 좋아졌다는 점입니다. 보통은 근거를 더 넣어 정확도를 사고 토큰을 지불하는데, 여기서는 필요한 문서를 곧바로 찾으니 헤매는 왕복이 줄었고 모델에게 넘기는 것도 문서 전체가 아니라 근거가 될 부분만으로 충분했습니다. 다만 저희가 만든 평가셋으로, 사내 문서를 대상으로 잰 값입니다. 문서를 모으고, 검색을 얹고, 명세를 다듬어 여기까지 온 결과입니다. 지금은 어디에 쓰이고 있나 1편에서 챗봇 대신 MCP를 만들기로 했다고 썼습니다. 질문을 받는 창구가 슬랙봇이든 사내 에이전트든 각자 쓰는 코딩 도구든 상관없고, 저희는 사내 지식에서 근거를 찾아 돌려주는 일만 맡겠다는 이야기였습니다. 프로젝트의 추상화된 전체 아키텍처 지금은 세 곳에 붙어 있습니다. 기술지원봇 은 Slack으로 들어온 기술 문의에 답변 초안을 달아주는 봇입니다. 문의가 등록되면 봇이 관련 문서를 찾아 초안을 만들고, 담당자가 확인한 뒤 문의자에게 전달합니다. 저희 MCP는 이 봇이 사내 문서를 찾을 때 쓰는 도구입니다. YAPP 은 사내 AI 에이전트 플랫폼입니다. 사내 도구들을 MCP로 연결해 두고, 사용자가 쓸 도구를 골라 웹이나 Slack에서 대화하듯 일을 맡기면 결과를 돌려받는 구조입니다. Atlas Retriever MCP도 그 목록에 올라가 있어, 사내 문서를 찾아야 할 때 골라 쓰면 됩니다. 개인 개발 환경 에도 붙여 씁니다. 사내 공용 서버가 떠 있으니 다른 MCP를 연결할 때처럼 클라이언트 설정에 주소만 추가하면 됩니다. 처음에는 저희 팀 문서만 넣고 시작했습니다. 지금은 전사 Confluence와 Jira가 대상이고, 지원봇도 팀 하나가 아니라 실 단위로 쓰이고 있습니다. 문서는 하루 세 번 증분으로 따라붙기 때문에, 어제 새로 쓴 가이드도 오늘 답변의 근거가 됩니다. 마치며 여기까지가 만든 것을 확인하고 내보내기까지의 이야기입니다. Langfuse로 무엇이 오갔는지 보이게 만들었고, 질문 유형을 일곱 가지로 나눠 평가셋을 만든 뒤 검색 지표와 LLM-as-a-judge 두 층으로 채점했습니다. FastMCP로 서빙하면서는 툴을 어떤 순서로 쓸지를 서버 instructions에 담았고, 끝으로 명세를 줄이고 다듬는 일로 정확도를 끌어올렸습니다. 물론 끝난 건 아닙니다. 임베딩 모델은 계속 세대가 바뀌고, 바뀔 때마다 전 문서를 다시 임베딩해야 합니다. 평가셋도 유형별로 더 촘촘히 채워야 하고, 사내 문서가 늘어날수록 무관한 문서가 섞여 들어오는 문제도 계속 손봐야 합니다. 다만 고칠 때마다 나아졌는지는 잴 수 있게 됐습니다. 이 시리즈를 이런 이야기로 시작했습니다. 같은 질문이 슬랙 DM으로 계속 돌아오고, 답을 아는 사람이 자리를 비우면 응답이 그대로 밀린다는 이야기였습니다. 지금은 그 자리에 초안이 먼저 놓입니다. 시리즈 구성 1편 : 프로젝트 개요와 데이터 파이프라인. 흩어진 문서를 모아 검색 가능한 형태로 바꾸기까지의 이야기입니다. 2편 : 검색을 얹기. 벡터 검색만으로 부족했던 이유와 LightRAG 도입, 그리고 의미 검색으로는 찾을 수 없는 것을 채우는 Navigator 이야기입니다. 3편 (이 글) : LLM Observability와 평가 파이프라인, FastMCP를 통한 툴 오케스트레이션과 MCP 서빙에 관한 이야기입니다. 읽어주셔서 감사합니다. 참고 Langfuse: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse FastMCP: https://github.com/PrefectHQ/fastmcp 사내 지식으로 Agentic RAG 만들기 (3/3) : 관측 가능한 RAG, 운영되는 도구로 was originally published in 여기어때 기술블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

content.source_text: British eyewear brand Cubitts has unveiled its first shop in Manchester , designed by locally based studio Youth to reflect the city's industrial and musical history without resorting to the obvious. Youth co-founders Oliver Collinge and Liam McGroarty planned the interior to reflect the present and future of the British city, with subtle references to the past rather than cliches. Shelving combines tubular steel uprights with dapple-textured glass shelves It includes a shelving display combining tubular steel uprights with dapple-textured glass shelves, a faceted oak counter housing a till and record player, and a pair of figurative sandstone sculptures by artist Richard Perry. The designers aimed to create a space "that feels both familiar and distinctly contemporary". Dimpled mirrors offer slightly cloudy reflections "Inspired by the city itself, the space draws on Manchester's culture and historic character, reinterpreted through a contemporary lens," they said. The approach reflects the brief set by Cubitts founder Tom Broughton "to make the space feel distinctly Cubitts without resorting to the usual Manchester shorthand". A faceted oak counter houses a till and record player "It was important that Cubitts Manchester was designed in Manchester, and not just deposited here," Broughton said. "Manchester does not need another London brand telling it how interesting it is. We're simply pleased to finally be here, and hope to make ourselves useful." Artworks include a pair of figurative sandstone sculptures by Richard Perry The store is located in Smithfield Buildings in the Northern Quarter, a collection of buildings that once housed the Affleck & Brown department store, dubbed the 'Harrods of the North'. After more than a decade looking at locations, Broughton and his team chose this one for its history as a supplier of cloth and made-to-measure garments. Read: EBBA Architects transforms former jellied-eel restaurant into eyewear store This aligns with Cubitts' own approach, with facilities for eye examinations, spectacle repairs and customisation made visible in the store. "Smithfield Buildings felt immediately right: a spectacle shop inside a former draper's department store, in a neighbourhood shaped by making, music and independent trade," said Broughton. The designers sourced a vintage bookcase made with salvaged timber from the HMS Foudroyant Waxed cotton curtains softly divide different areas in tribute to Affleck & Brown's legacy, while other additions include a vintage revolving bookcase. Produced by Manchester cabinetmakers Goodall, Lamb and Heighway, this century-old piece was made with salvaged timber from the Royal Navy ship HMS Foudroyant. A wall of material samples celebrates Cubitts' customisation options Artworks also hint at industrial production; a seamstress is depicted in a painting by artist Francis Hoyland, while a cubist gouache by artist Marcel Gille depicts a forge worker. Completing the design are dimpled mirrors that offer slightly cloudy reflections and a collection of records spanning soul, jazz, punk and electronica. Cubitts Manchester is located in Smithfield Buildings in the Northern Quarter Cubitts Manchester is the brand's 21st location, following others that include the peep-show-inspired Cubitts Soho and the art-deco-style Cubitts Leeds . The company also just unveiled a new headquarters in London's King's Cross , in a historic building that began as a working stable for the Crosse & Blackwell Vinegar Works, before being converted into an office for a publishing house. The photography is courtesy of Cubitts. The post Youth avoids Manchester cliches for city's first Cubitts eyewear store appeared first on Dezeen .
content.original_title: Youth avoids Manchester cliches for city's first Cubitts eyewear store

content.source_text: This article is a sponsored by ProtoPie There’s a moment in almost every usability session where a participant pauses at the login screen, types something, and glances up: checking whether they’re “doing it right.” That pause is a clear sign. They’ve already clocked that this isn’t a real app, and every data point collected after that moment is filtered through that awareness. In financial product testing, the problem is sharper. Finance users are trained to notice when something feels off: a balance that doesn’t add up, a field that accepts anything. When a banking prototype skips real authentication, participants don’t just disengage; they stop mid-session to flag it. The team walks away with findings that reflect how users behave in a demonstration, not in a real product. The fix is narrower than you’d think. Identify the moment where participant trust is established and make that interaction real. In a banking app, that moment is the login. This tutorial builds it: credentials that validate, a live error state, and a biometric animation that feels native — no code required. What We’re Building: A Login That Behaves Like A Shipped Product The login flow, built around Pie Bank, a mobile banking prototype, includes functional text inputs, a masked password field, credential validation, a live error state, and a Face ID animation timed to feel indistinguishable from iOS. What you’ll need: A login UI from Figma (or any supported design tool) ProtoPie Studio — free to start , everything in this tutorial works on the free plan A Lottie file for the Face ID animation ( this one is what we used) The finished Pie Bank prototype file — download it to follow alongside, or use it as a reference after you build Step 1: Import From Figma Choose Scene, Not Flattened In Figma, open the ProtoPie plugin with your login frame selected and choose Scene when exporting. Flattened collapses everything into a single image; Scene preserves your layer hierarchy so every element arrives in ProtoPie as a separate, targetable layer. Before moving on: rename every layer meaningfully. “Input Username” not “Rectangle 14”. You’ll reference these names in formulas: vague names compound into real time lost. Step 2: Swap Static Fields For Inputs That Actually Accept Text ProtoPie’s native Input layer accepts real keyboard entry: participants type actual text, not tap a placeholder. Go to Text → Input , drag an Input layer onto your canvas, and nest it inside your username field group. Match it visually: placeholder text Username , background fill and font to match your design. Hit preview. Click the field. Type. That’s the prototype starting to behave like an app rather than depicting one. Rename this layer Input Username , duplicate it, and nest the copy inside your password field group. Step 3: One Property Change Masks The Password On the duplicated layer, change placeholder text to Password and set Type to Text Password . ProtoPie handles the masking: no custom logic needed. Preview both fields: username shows text, password shows dots. It already feels real, and you haven’t written a single condition. Step 4: Build The Destination Scene Before Wiring Navigation Add a new scene, even a blank one. The most common sequencing mistake in ProtoPie is trying to wire a navigation response before a destination exists. Create it first. Step 5: Wire The Button: It Works, But It Still Lets Everyone Through Select Log In , add a Tap trigger, set response to Jump , target your dashboard scene, transition Slide in from right to left . Preview and tap. It navigates: but for any input, including nothing. The prototype is still lying. The next two steps are the fix. Step 6: Add Variables So The Prototype Remembers What Was Typed At the bottom-left of ProtoPie, add two Text type variables: username and password . Bind each to its input layer with a formula: input("Input Username").text input("Input Password").text Enable the debug icons: green overlays will show live variable values as you type. When you see your keystrokes appear in real time, the binding is confirmed. Step 7: Add A Condition So Only Valid Credentials Get Through Go back to the Tap trigger on the login button. Add a Condition with two rules, both must be true: username equals `alex.c@gmail.com ` password equals ABC123 Move the Jump response inside this condition. Wrong credentials, empty fields, wrong format: none get through. Participants now have to actually log in. That single constraint changes the texture of every test session that follows. Step 8: Build The Error State, The Interaction Most Prototypes Skip Find your error message layer, rename it Error Text , set initial opacity to 0 . Add a second condition (the inverse of the first), and inside it, a Change Property response setting Error Text opacity to 100 . Wrong credentials: error appears. Correct credentials: dashboard. Two outcomes: which is what makes this testable, not just demonstrable. Step 9: Add the Face ID Animation, The Detail That Makes Testers Ask “Is This Real” Go to Media , drag a Lottie layer onto canvas, load your Face ID file, and position it off-screen above the iPhone frame. On your Login with Face ID button, add a Tap trigger (rename it Tap Face ID ) with four responses in sequence: Move : Lottie container to Y: 60 Playback : Seek: time 0s (resets so it always plays from the start) Playback: Play : Lottie file Jump : to dashboard Step 10: Stagger The Timing, This Is What Makes It Feel Native Without delays, all four responses fire at once and the scene jumps before the animation plays. Add offsets: Response Delay Move 0s Seek 0s Play 0.5s Jump 1s Enable Reset selected scenes on Jump: without it, navigating back leaves the animation stuck at Y: 60 . Preview: tap Face ID, animation drops in, plays, screen transitions. A biometric login indistinguishable from the real thing. You can download Pie Bank, Chapter 1: Login Flow and explore it freely. A Login This Real Changes What You Can Learn From Your Prototype When authentication actually works, the error state becomes a genuine research touchpoint: do users understand the message, do they retry, do they reach for Face ID instead? These are questions a faked login can’t answer. In stakeholder reviews, the flow speaks for itself. In engineering handoff, the interaction panel documents the behavior (conditional logic, variable bindings, timing) so engineers see intent, not interpretation. This is why FinTech teams invest in login fidelity even when the login isn’t the feature being tested. It’s where participant trust is established. Get it right, and everything downstream produces better signal. This tutorial is part of the FinTech Prototyping with ProtoPie series on the ProtoPie blog. The series builds Pie Bank from the ground up across four chapters, covering the dashboard, money transfer logic, and camera integration. If this tutorial was useful, the rest of the series goes further.
content.original_title: Your Prototype Is Not Being Honest With Your Users (And Here’s How To Fix It)

content.source_text: New York studio Surrane Design has outfitted Thai restaurant Hommali in New York with a terracotta floor, a central "courtyard" space and personal items of the founders to create a space that resembles a traditional Thai house. Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives chef Chattchakorn "Benz" Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee "Air" Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak "Picha" Srigungvarl after they moved to New York City and met in the hospitality scene. Surrane Design has completed a Thai restaurant in the West Village The restaurant contains an eight-seat bar, a 20-seat dining den, a semi-private mezzanine and auxiliary spaces such as a wine room and dry-age room where ducks and other ferments are on display. Surrane Design layered the space with a rich assortment of textures and patterns, such as dark wood millwork, a marbled bar top and artwork sourced from Bangkok's Chatuchak Weekend Market. It brings together a rich assortment of textures and colours informed by Thailand According to the team, its palette of browns and greens was informed by the life cycle of a rice plant. "The color palette is inspired by the stages of the rice plant: fresh green for young leaves, golden yellow for mature stalks, earthy brown for paddy soil, soft beige for rice husks, and warm cream white for polished rice," said the team. Personal items from the ownership team line a partition It was designed to resemble a traditional Thai house, where the central dining den and mezzanine above recall a courtyard, and the terracotta floor also calls to the vernacular architecture of the country. Visitors are greeted with a rice plant light installation at the doorway and enter by the bar, which is clad in a sandy fluted tile with seats upholstered in leather and velvet. Stairs lead to a mezzanine with additional seating Two booths sit in front of the main dining space, which is tucked beneath the mezzanine. Curtains and open shelving separate the two spaces. Personal items from the ownership team, such as vintage Thai cookbooks from the late 1960s and early 1970s and other objects "one would expect to find in a living room" line the shelves. Small bamboo sculptures by Thai artist Korakot Aromdee are also peppered throughout the space. Read: OMA's Oberon restaurant at the New Museum is "hidden in plain sight" Wood-lined stairs lead to the mezzanine above, which contains additional seating concealed behind a frosted glass railing. A large skylight hangs above the space and sits over a large dining table. Banquets and an off-white white wallpaper embossed with 3D-printed plants also line the space. Like below, a curtain can be drawn across the length of the space to provide additional separation. A large skylight hangs above the space Hommali will serve contemporary takes on traditional Thai dishes created under Benz, such as a seafood cocktail with razor clams imbued with the hot and sour notes of tom yum and the Tomato, "a michelada-meets-spritz with a Singaporean rice wine base accompanied by a Thai chile tincture." Surrane Design is an independent design studio based in Brooklyn by partners Bud Nitaya and Yoon Her. Other recently opened spaces in the West Village include Love Thy Neighbour next to The Stonewall Inn and The Cherry Lane Theatre The photography is by Hommali The post Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York appeared first on Dezeen .
